title: Old government tech poses cybersecurity risks, warns GAO official
text:
Across the U.S., some federal computer systems used to collect taxes, support national security and deliver public services date back to the era when NASA first sent astronauts to the moon.
The government spends at least $100 billion on IT systems every year. About 20% of that is used to develop new technology. The rest goes to operate and maintain the outdated technology currently in use, according to Dave Hinchman, director of information technology and cybersecurity at the Government Accountability Office.
Recent tech outages involving federal government agencies, including the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Security Agency, raised questions about the reliability of government technology.
Officials said the outagesweren't related or caused by cyberattacks. Cybersecurity experts say AI is exposing software flaws faster, prompting updates that can sometimes cause disruptions themselves.
Hinchman toldMorning Editionhis agency has identified critical federal computer systems in need of modernization.
"We found systems in agriculture, commerce, defense, energy, Health and Human Services — really across the gamut," he said.
The GAO operates at the request of Congress. Hinchman said specific congressional action to compel agencies to improve their modernization efforts would be "very helpful" for cybersecurity measures. The specific outdated systemswere not specified in its reportbecause doing so could expose them to security threats, Hinchman said.
One example of an outdated system, according to Hinchman, is the Internal Revenue Service's Individual Master File, which is used to maintain individual taxpayers' records. The technology was first introduced during the Apollo era, when NASA was sending astronauts to the moon, Hinchman said.
Nicknamed IMF, the master file is a legacy software application and database system established in 1970. That exact same system is still in use today, Hinchman said, noting that the programming language it uses hasn't been taught in schools for decades.
"It's become increasingly expensive to find people who have experience in that language just to maintain the code," Hinchman said.
He said a lot of people argue, "if it works, don't fix it," but realistically this system makes it more difficult to respond to changes in the tax code, view taxpayers' accounts in real time and ensure data security.
IMF isn't the only outdated tech used by the IRS. Hinchman said the customer service system requires employees to log into at least eight different systems to gain access to the information needed to answer customer questions, which means longer wait times and less efficient answers to pressing tax-related questions.
Back when data centers were used to house information within agency networks, accessing sensitive information often required physical access to the facility, Hinchman said. Today, keeping that data safe is harder as more government services move online.
"As we move into a greater interconnected age, increasingly government services are being moved online, and that's how vulnerabilities are created," Hinchman said.
When personal data is all stored and accessible online, Hinchman said it's a lot easier to gain access to private information, especially when data is stored in outdated systems.
"If your tax information is hacked or your Social Security information is hacked, you have the potential release of personally identifiable information to someone with bad intentions," Hinchman said.
"That can have a very real effect on an individual because of these older systems that can't be updated with modern cybersecurity protocols."
The simple answer: sometimes it's just too expensive to modernize.
"Our work has found that sometimes it's hard for individuals who are leading a modernization effort at a specific agency to get budgetary support for what they want to do," Hinchman said.
Even when existing systems need upgrades, agency officials can struggle to justify spending on modernization over other priorities, he added.
"And I think it's hard sometimes, internal to agencies, to make the business case for why system X really needs to be modernized over some other potential use for that same pool of resources."
For now, the government is spending billions keeping old technology running instead of replacing it. And with more services moving online, the risks aren't going away anytime soon.
The radio interview was edited by Arezou Rezvani. The digital version was edited by Majd Al-Waheidi.

title: Nvidia board says it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO
text:
Nvidia said it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang, amid a push by the former CEO's allies to return him to lead the chipmaker he cofounded.
Huang "voluntarily resigned" on Nov. 12 after disclosing "personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms," board chair Harvey Jones said on the company's earnings call on Tuesday afternoon. "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."
Earlier on Tuesday, Huang had said he would return to lead the company he cofounded if Nvidia's board  allowed him to. Huang also agreed to appear before Congress to answer questions about the national security scandals swirling around the company.
"I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," Huang wrote in a statementposted on social media. "I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation."
Huangstepped downfrom the company last week afteracknowledgingthat he had been unfaithful to his wife.News reportshave tied him to a woman who U.S. intelligence officials say wasrecruited by China's spy agency, as well as withanother womanwho is an executive at Nvidia. NPR has not independently confirmed those reports.
Huang said he would be "honored" to return to the company if Nvidia's board agreed. His comments came as some in Silicon Valley have tried to argue that Huang was pushed out of the company too quickly, and circulated a petition to "stand with Jensen."
"We don't want rushes to judgment. We don't want political pressure from the left or the right to force a board into action before we've even taken the time to turn over the cards and learn what was done," said Brad Gerstner, the founder and CEO of Altimeter Capital, an investor in Nvidia, at Semafor's Silicon Valley and the World conference on Monday.
Huang and Nvidia's general counsel Tim Teter willanswer questions behind closed doorsfrom the House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence Committees and the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party on Dec. 1st and 2nd.
Lawmakers say they want answers about Nvidia's role in alleged chip smuggling and efforts to evade export controls meant to block China from accessing the most advanced U.S. AI chips. They will also ask Huang about his involvement withAlice Huang, who was an executive withMegaspeed, a Singapore-based company that was a major customer for Nvidia's chips. In a statement emailed to NPR, Megaspeed said it "conducts legitimate and lawful business," and that Alice Huang left the company in 2025, but that it is conducting an internal investigation.
Nvidia's board saidon Tuesday it had formed a committee to oversee the company's national security policies, compliance with U.S. export controls, and risk management of global trade.
On Monday, the U.S. Commerce Departmentannounced new rulesto prevent remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips and servers, closing a loophole that may have let Chinese companies remotely access advanced Nvidia chips through overseas data centers. The Commerce Department and Justice Department also announced Monday thatthe DOJ is conducting a criminal investigationof Megaspeed.
Nvidia sought to reassure investors about the company's future during its third-quarter earnings call on Tuesday.
"Our ambition will not change. Our passion to innovate will not change. And our commitment to customers, partners and shareholders will not change," said Colette Kress, the company's chief financial officer who is serving as interim CEO while the board finds a permanent leader.
Quarterly sales doubled to a record $115.8 billion and profit also doubled to $65.3 billion from a year ago. The company said it was raising its forecast for sales growth next year.
Nvidia shares were up 5% in after-hours trading on Tuesday. The company's stock price has dropped more than 16% since Huang admitting having an extramarital affair earlier this month.

title: I'm a human doctor with human intelligence. But I sure do like my AI notetaker
text:
Dr. Mara Gordon, a family physician in Camden, N.J., answers reader health questions monthly. Send in your question to:thrive@npr.org.
Question: My doctor has started recording our office visits with an artificial intelligence scribe. She says it helps write notes in my medical record. I said yes when she asked if I was comfortable with it, but in hindsight I feel a little freaked out. Should I be worried about AI listening in on my private medical conversations?
Answer:AI scribes are all the rage in medicine right now. Doctorsare using themto take notes everywhere from the gynecologist's office to the emergency room.
I admit I've been an eager adopter in my own primary care practice. I use an app on my phone that records my conversation with a patient and then uses AI to write a preliminary summary for the medical record.
Itsaves me time. But more importantly, I like using it because it helps me focus more fully on my patient. When I use the AI scribe, I don't have to talk and take notes at the same time – I can actually make eye contact with my patient rather than staring at the computer screen.
But I totally get why people feel uncomfortable with the technology. I share my patients' concerns about privacy and how AI scribes might impact the doctor-patient relationship.
I also worry that corporate health systems will put pressure on doctors to use any time we save with an AI scribe to squeeze in evenmorepatients.
And like many people, I worry that artificial intelligence might one day put me out of a job!
Here's what you need to know.
When I use an AI scribe during a primary care visit, I first ask the patient if they're comfortable using the service. If the patient says yes, I start recording using an app on my smartphone. I usually set it down on the desk in the exam room.
The scribe uses a technology called "automatic speech recognition" which records our conversation and automatically distinguishes between the doctor's and patient's voices. (Sometimes, when the patient has a family member accompanying him, the app needs to distinguish between three – or more! – voices.)
When the visit ends, the recording is then transcribed. A large language model – the kind of AI technology that powers ChatGPT, but specifically geared toward medicine – converts the raw transcript into a medical note. These notes follow a standard format that is specific to the speciality and the type of visit. They reflect what the patient told the doctor, physical exam findings, and the doctor's medical decision-making.
There are lots of AI scribes on the market, ranging from products embedded within the electronic medical record to free apps a doctor can download on her phone. Most scribes use a smartphone's recording capabilities to "listen in" on the conversation, although there are some that use a desktop computer or a separate recording device.
I use my personal smartphone for this purpose, as do many physicians I know. I downloaded the AI scribe software as an app on my phone. This causes occasional hiccups. For example, I've gotten notification pings from my book club's group chat while recording a patient visit – which made me make sure to put the phone in "do not disturb" mode whenever I'm using it for patient care.
Even though I use my personal phone for scribing patient visits, our conversations aren't stored on my device.They're uploaded directly to a HIPAA-compliant cloud, where the data is then transcribed into the AI-generated clinical note. Most scribe systems then delete the recording and the note after a set period of time.
HIPAA-compliance is an important feature of all AI scribe services. It means that the computer program was designed in accordance with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, a federal law designed to protect patients' privacy.
The software company is responsible for safeguarding the data at every step of the process, from recording to generating notes. AI scribe companies encrypt the data, control who has access to it, and have systems to protect against "data breaches." It also means these companies are liable if the data is leaked.
Recently, I saw a patient who had metastatic cancer. Despite multiple conversations about his diagnosis with me, his oncologist, and his surgeon, he did not believe he had cancer. I had even – with his permission – called his spouse to tell her what was going on. He still did not accept it.
This kind of tricky clinical situation comes up on occasion, and the AI scribe didnotget it right. Rather than reflecting the nuances of our conversation, the note that the scribe produced simply said that the patient had been misdiagnosed.
I often catch other errors that the software makes, like mistaking a patient's gender or age. Alarmingly, these scribes are also known for mistaking "I do" statements with "I do not." In medicine, this can be critical: The difference between "I do have chest pain" and "I do not have chest pain" can be a matter of life and death.
To better understand how AI scribes can contribute to errors in the medical record, I talked toDr. Eileen Kim, an assistant professor of internal medicine at the University of California San Diego. Kim specializes in clinical informatics and thinks a lot about how AI might shape the future of medicine.
"You have a doctor who's overburdened, seeing way too many patients," she said. "They have this AI tool that's offered to them that seems like a great solution, but they don't have time to adequately review everything. It goes into the chart. Then you have another AI tool that's reading through all these notes. But they're wrong. And then it just propagates errors throughout the chart."
In my work caring for patients, I come across erroneous information in the electronic health record all the time. It's hard to know how much is related to AI and how much is caused by human error. But I think Dr. Kim is right to worry that AI scribes might make the problem worse.
As the doctor caring for my patient, I'm ultimately the one responsible for the content of the AI-generated note, so I always read them carefully before clicking "sign" and adding them to the medical record. Most AI scribe software makes doctors sign a user agreement stating doctors are liable for everything they write in the medical record, even if a scribe helps them with it.
When the AI-generated notes are factually accurate, I almost always end up editing them to make my clinical decision-making more clear. I'm happy to have robots help me with my administrative tasks, but I still take pride in being a human doctor with human intelligence!
Many AI scribes can only be used with English-speaking patients. Health equity advocates say they fear this means unequal access to the technology, which could further widen health disparities.
For example, the scribe allows me to look more at my patient and less at my computer, which might make a patient feel more comfortable disclosing a stigmatizing health concern. Or the opposite might be true, too: A patient fearful that an AI company is "listening in" to our conversation might be afraid to share sensitive information, which in turn could affect the quality of their medical care.
As a security feature, most AI scribe companies delete the recorded conversations within a set period of time. This is to protect patient privacy and also protect doctors from lawsuits. There is widespread concern in health care that the transcriptions could be used in medical malpractice lawsuits.
Butsome researchers call the recordings "digital gold"that could be used to assess the quality of AI-generated medical notes or even to study broader questions about physician-patient communication.
For example, I'd love to know how other doctors handle tricky conversations with patients who are fearful of vaccines. There are theoretical best practices, but analyzing hundreds of thousands of office-visit transcripts could help doctors learn what actually works best in real life.
For now, recordings of regular doctors' appointments — unless you've been enrolled in a research study — are not used for research purposes.
Most of my patients readily agree when I ask if it's OK to use the AI scribe software, but occasionally my patients have concerns. They worry that the data isn't really secure or that it could be used to identify them in the future.
If a patient doesn't want to use the AI scribe, it's no problem. I just take notes on the computer while they talk — it's what I've done for years before the AI scribes became available.
Opting out of AI in medicine more broadly may prove to be tricky.
"It's just everywhere," said Kim, the clinical information specialist. "It would be impossible to separate. We use it throughout the healthcare system."
Software that relies on machine learning is used for billing, for clinical decision-making, and for communication between the doctor's office and patients.
AI is often used in risk calculators, like clinical tools that estimate a patient's risk of, say, heart disease based on variables like cholesterol levels and blood pressure. AI is also common in "early warning" systems that notify clinicians their patients might be vulnerable to high-risk conditions like sepsis, based on vital signs and lab values.
Kim says it's basically impossible for patients to opt out entirely from having AI involved in their medical care, "unless you're so healthy that no risk calculators ever come near you," she said.
I asked Kim — a primary care doctor like me — if she thought AI would replace us in the coming years. If the AI scribe could learn to ask the same questions I do, could it generate a treatment plan as good — or better — as the one I recommend?
Kim thought AI might change how patients experience primary care. (Possibly for the better, she said, if AI scribes allow doctors to focus more on their patients and less on the computer!)
But ultimately, she thinks human intelligence is critical in medicine.
"It looks really good because it's really good at sounding like us, and it's really good at pretending to be us," she said. "But it's still just pretending in a way. There's no real brain."
I agree. I think the AI scribe technology has the potential to do both good and harm for health care. But the core of medicine is the relationship I have with my patients. No robot can replace that.
Dr. Mara Gordon is a family physician in Camden, NJ. Find her newsletterYour Doctor Friend on Substack.

title: Does locking up a student's cellphone improve test scores? A new study suggests so
text:
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.
The rise of smartphones in the U.S. coincided with a dramatic slide in K-12 students' reading and math achievement. Now,new researchsuggests putting students' phones in locked pouches during the school day may help restore some of those historic losses.
"Around 2013, U.S. students started losing 2-3 weeks of learning each year," says Harvard University's Tom Kane, one of the new study's co-authors. "It's been a slow leak that, over time, has put U.S. 8th graders almost a year behind. Strict cellphone bans seem to plug about half of that leak."
Or the equivalent of 1-2 weeks of learning a year, according to the study released Tuesday. That's a small but, according to Kane, statistically significant improvement.
"That could add up over time, just as the initial declines did," adds Dartmouth College's Douglas Staiger, another co-author.
The study's authors say it is the first nationwide analysis of student-level test scores in math and reading both before and after schools enforced locked-pouch cellphone bans. It was a joint effort between Harvard's Center for Education Policy Research, Dartmouth and NWEA, a K-12 testing and research organization.
Kane, Staiger and their teams analyzed a nationwide sample of more than 3 million elementary-, middle- and high-school students over the past five school years, comparing the test scores in schools that adopted phone pouches to the scores at similar schools that did not.
Not only did strict cellphone bans appear to trigger small learning gains, the researchers say, those gains didn't seem to fade out after the first year of implementation. Instead, Kane says, the gains appeared to continue, year after year – at least up to three years after adoption.
Tuesday's headline finding, that locking phones during the school day led to small but statistically significant improvements in math and reading scores, comes with an important caveat:
Aseparate study, from April, found that these pouches had "close to zero" impact on student test scores – and if there was a benefit, it wasnotstatistically significant.
"Overall, we didn't find evidence of meaningful achievement gains," says Brian Jacob, a co-author of that April study anda professor of education policy at the University of Michigan.
What should we make of these seemingly contradictory results?
Both are large-scale studies by well-respected teams of researchers. The April study has been peer-reviewed; the more recent study has not.
Both studies similarly focused on schools' adoption of lockable pouches made by the for-profit company Yondr. According to Tuesday's paper, more than 3,300 schools nationwide began using the pouches between the '19-'20 and '25-'26 school years. Typically, schools that use the pouches require that students put their phones in them at the beginning of the day and don't get them back until the end of the school day, when the pouches are unlocked by a school administrator with a special magnetic device.
But the two studies also differ in key ways. The April study pooled school-level mean test scores at several thousand Yondr-adopting schools, while Tuesday's study used student-level scores at the 844 schools that use both Yondr pouches and tests administered by NWEA.
Simply put, the study released Tuesday had more fine-grain, student-level data, but the study released in April was able to examine a much larger sample of schools.
But the two studies' findings also aren't as different as they may seem. Jacob and his co-authors did find statistically significant gains with Yondr pouches in high school math. It's just that those gains were offset by ban-related learninglossesin middle school.
Overall, Jacob says, the new study "is encouraging. And if [the benefit] really persists and accumulates over time, it really could be a meaningful benefit. I think we'll just have to wait and see if that happens."
Another co-author of that April study, Tom Dee, a professor at Stanford University's Graduate School of Education, says of Tuesday's findings, "I hope they are right that these very small test score gains will aggregate and add up over time. However, I'm not comfortable making that extrapolation from estimates that are small, sensitive and based on just a few years of phone bans."
Taken together, Dee says, he considers the results from these early studies into cellphone bans "largely disappointing," and insists "we need continued study on this topic."
Kane sees the results differently. Even if the benefit is small, he argues, relative to the cost – roughly $25 per student – these pouches still make financial sense for schools. "That's still a lot less than having to pay teachers for an extra week or two of instruction."
For nearly a quarter-century, from 1990 to 2013, math achievement among fourth- and eighth-graders rose steadily. Reading scores also improved.
Then around 2013, student test scores began a sustained tumble that continued through the COVID-19 pandemic and has only recently begun to slow. For years, politicians and pundits blamed pandemic-era school closures for the losses, but the data tells a different story.
"Particularly in reading, test scores were going down for four to six years before the pandemic," Stanford University researcher Sean Reardontold NPR earlier this year. "In fact, you wouldn't really know there was a pandemic effect if you just looked at the last 10 or 12 years of test scores. There's been just a steady kind of decline regardless of the pandemic."
Which raises the question: What happened around 2013?
Possible explanations abound. The federal government began stepping back from holding schools accountable for low test scores. Many schools also saw funding cuts in the wake of the Great Recession.
This new study is the latest to make the case that the mass adoption of cell phones by children and teens also helped fuel those test score declines.
The researchers note that, in 2011, fewer than a quarter of teen students had access to smartphones. By 2018, 95% did. And similar rates in other industrialized countries coincided with similar student achievement declines.
Now, Kane says, he wants to study students' smartphone and social media useoutsideof school.

title: California sues OpenAI over hacking risks
text:
California sued OpenAI Monday, alleging that the frontier AI company failed to protect the public from its systems' advanced cyber capabilities. The lawsuit stems from OpenAI's agents' attack on open-source software platform Hugging Face over the summer but also touches on a wide range of other related incidents tied to the company's agents acting without authorization.
"Just because the technology is new or rapidly evolving doesn't mean the people behind it are above the law," said California Attorney General Rob Bonta during a press conference. "Whether it's a car or a toy, the law is simple: don't build or test things that can hurt people without proper safeguards." The lawsuit cited potential concerns about cyberattacks "on power grids, emergency infrastructure, hospital systems, and financial institutions."
In thecomplaint, California alleged that OpenAI misled the public about how unsafe its products are. The state said the company admitted to the attorney general's office that "it lost control of its autonomous AI agents over 80 times during testing."
That number is higher than what OpenAI has so far disclosed publicly and more than whatoutside researchershave independently discovered, but OpenAI has otherwise provided little information, California said. The state also accused OpenAI of poor security practices, stonewalling the state's investigation into the company and discouraging employees from speaking up about safety.
In a statement to NPR, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the lawsuit "appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab" and that the company has "engaged—and will continue to engage—constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry."
After the most notorious of cyber incidents involving OpenAI's agents –the attack on Hugging Faceover the summer – the companyadmittedthat it did not monitor its agents in ways its own researchers deemed important. Since then, outside researchers as well as OpenAI itself have found more incidents in which AI agents have interacted with websites and communicated with each other on the internet in ways that OpenAI did not intend. The lawsuit mentions these events as well as other incidents that OpenAI starteddisclosingvoluntarily to the public.
Other AI companies have also had to wrestle with their systems behaving in unexpected and undesirable ways. Anthropic and Meta have both said they found that their AI systems have hacked into places they shouldn't have.Major AI companies have since signed onto anagreementorganized by the White House to develop AI responsibly, but the agreement is nonbinding.
Drawing from reports including from OpenAI's own disclosures, California alleges that the top AI company has engaged in unfair competition and created a public nuisance. It asked the court to stop the company from further engaging in such activities and order it to pay monetary damages.

title: U.S. tightens controls on remote access to AI technology amid Nvidia fallout
text:
The U.S. government hasannounced a ruleto prevent remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips and servers, closing a loophole that could let adversarial governments access American AI technology through overseas data centers.
The move comes amid the fallout at Nvidia, the world's dominant producer of AI chips, following revelations that CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials suspected of being a Chinese intelligence operative. NPR has not independently verified the claims. Huangstepped downas CEO last week.
Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, is a former executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data center company. Jensen Huang haspersonally lobbiedPresident Trump to loosen restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China. It is not known if Alice Huang influenced this activity.
The rapid advancement in cloud computing and AI infrastructure has made it possible to access advanced U.S. computing capabilities remotely, including through data centers located outside countries subject to U.S. export restrictions, the U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) said in astatementon Monday.
The rule is designed to reinforce existing restrictions on access to sensitive American AI technology through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in other countries, which could threaten national security
However, a loophole existed where Chinese companies could still access those chips remotely, despite U.S. restrictions on their physical sale to China.
"The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten U.S. national security," the BIS statement said.
The government refers to artificial intelligence as "super intelligence" following anexecutive ordersigned by President Trump in September.
Since October 2022, U.S. companies have typically needed a BIS export license to sell advanced computing chips meeting specified technical thresholds to China, including Hong Kong and Macau. These restrictions covered advanced Nvidia chips, some high-performance semiconductor components, and certain AI computing systems.
Megaspeed is based in Singapore and operates facilities in Malaysia.
"Megaspeed conducts legitimate and lawful business. The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation," the company said in a statement emailed to NPR and other news organizations on Sunday.
In a joint statement late Monday, the Department of Commerce and the Department of Justice said that U.S. authorities had launched a criminal investigation into Megaspeed in 2025 after conducting an "on-site, in-person, end-use check" at the Singaporean-based company and interviewing its then CEO Alice Huang.
"Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation against Megaspeed," the statement said.
In the statementpostedon X, the two departments said they "will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred."
The statement also provided a timeline of the ongoing probe against Megaspeed, detailing how the investigation was initiated in 2024 by the Department of Commerce "for potential export control violations" after "identifying suspicious activity through proactive monitoring of potential sensitive semiconductor diversion." It said that the probe involved a request to Nvidia to provide records of "direct or indirect sales" to the company. According to the statement, by June 2025 Nvidia had placed Megaspeed on their "no sell" list.
Prior to the Nvidia scandal, the Trump administration had resisted imposing additional regulations to prevent foreign access to American AI technology.
The Biden administration had written a framework designed to control worldwide distribution of advanced AI chips on January 15, 2025 – five days before Trump's inauguration. In May 2025, Trump's Commerce Departmentannouncedit would not enforce the rule and intended to rescind it, calling it "ill-conceived and counterproductive."
Biden's framework would have also limited access to AI chips by countries considered security risks, required licenses for certain chip exports, and created restrictions on the power of advanced models and computing infrastructure.
The New York Timesreportedthat Trump was first briefed by intelligence officials about Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy in October 2025. Both Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick are expected to testify before Congress this month and next month and there will likely be further investigations into what Trump knew about the affair when the Democrats take control of Congress in January 2027, Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-NY, told NPR.
"We need to get the facts investigated, bring in individuals to give us as much information as possible under oath, so that we can get to the bottom of why this happened, how it occurred, and how we could prevent this type of compromise from happening again," said Clarke.

title: U.N. talks seek to rein in 'killer robots' as fears over AI weapons grow
text:
GENEVA — Negotiations on possible rules for the use of lethal autonomous weapons, also known as 'killer robots' are underway at the United Nations in Geneva.
Supporters of controls on autonomous weapons say this week's U.N. conference on Certain Conventional Weapons (or CCW), which meets just once every five years, is the last best chance to agree rules before it is too late.
Warfare technology has advanced rapidly in the last few years, with some experts warning that the world is just months away from havingweaponsthat can choose targets and make the decision to kill autonomously.
In Ukraine and Gaza, AI-assisted weapons have already been used to take out targets, with Ukrainian civilians reporting being 'hunted' by drones as they shop or go to school. But these are still controlled remotely by humans.
Humanitarian organizations say the decision to kill – and responsibility for that choice – must stay in human hands. Ahead of this week's meeting, the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross and thePopehave all called for legally binding rules. U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned that allowing fully autonomous weapons to kill would be 'crossing a moral red line'.
The Red Cross is especially worried that existing rules of war – the Geneva Conventions – cannot be fully respected by autonomous weapons. War is often chaotic and confusing, and the situation can change rapidly. Under the Conventions, soldiers who are wounded or in the process of surrendering can no longer be targeted.
Georgia Hinds, a legal adviser with the Red Cross, worries that autonomous weapons will not be able to distinguish between a soldier who is still fighting, one who is wounded and one who wants to surrender.
'The risk is that, based on the technology we are seeing, they are not able to understand in the same way that a human is the contextual signals. And so the risks are incredibly high that there will be a misidentification of a target," Hinds says.
Meanwhile, human rights groups warn that the technology behind AI-assisted weapons is becoming increasingly cheap and easy to use. The more it is adopted by the military, the greater the danger of proliferation and its use by terrorist groups or law enforcement agencies in repressive regimes. Intheory, a swarm of autonomous drones could be programmed to kill everyone wearing a red sweater, everyone carrying a poster or even everyone speaking a certain language.
Many of the countries now meeting in Geneva take such concerns very seriously. At least 50, including Ireland, Italy, Brazil, Mexico, France and Germany, are calling for a strict timetable to agree on binding rules governing autonomous weapons.
But among states that are already developing and using semi-autonomous weapons, there is pushback. The United States, Russia and Israel have indicated they are set to oppose legally binding rules, with Washington proposing a five-year timetable to draft non-binding guidelines instead.
The U.S. is traditionally a late adopter of international treaties. It did not ratify the Ottawa Convention on landmines, for example, although it did, over time, stop deploying them and reduce its stockpiles.
Under President Trump, doubts about international law have grown. Washington has imposed sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court, and just this weekend, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in a keynote speech to the Federalist Society, warned against  "quoting laws to men with swords."
The problem for states meeting in Geneva is that U.N. negotiations on limiting specific weapons are supposed to be conducted by consensus. This was achieved in 1995, when countries agreed to a ban on blinding lasers, but other agreements have proved elusive. With landmines, countries frustrated by the delay finally took negotiations outside the U.N. process to create the Ottawa Convention.
This week, there may be a compromise: a longer or even open-ended negotiating period to come up with rules that individual states can adopt as binding or non-binding. For diplomats supporting such a solution, it is a way to ensure at least some progress. For campaigners, it is less than ideal, with one likening it to kicking a very dangerous can down the road.

title: How the movement against data centers has gone global
text:
At a demonstration in downtown Zaragoza in Spain, grandmothers, moms with babies in carriers, teenagers filled an entire avenue as they called to stop a Microsoft data center from being built beside a beloved local forest.
Videos of the loud opposition to data centers in the United States helped inspire university student Monica Gracia to show up.
"I think that's one of the reasons why this place is so full of people," said Gracia.
While many environmental problems are often very local, most of the push to build data centers around the world comes from U.S. tech giants. So opponents fighting new data centers are teaming up across continents.
"We have connections with of course the USA, Africa, Australia and even some parts of Asia," said Aurora Gomez, a Spanish activist. "We are coordinated and we are together."
Gomez founded the group Tu Nube Seca Mi Rio, which translates to 'Your Cloud Dries My River,' to stop a data centre in her home town, Talavera La Reina in Spain.
"It was meant to be a weeklong campaign to raise local awareness," she told NPR. "But it just caught fire, because there are so many data centers coming to Spain and to every part of the world."
Gomez said she now fields dozens of emails a day from residents of communities where data centers are planned.
She was recently part of a wider European effort that coordinated a series of protests against data centers in 15 countries over two days under the banner "Stop Dirty Data Centres," demanding an immediate moratorium on large-scale projects.
"We are gaining so much traction - our narratives are being spread around the world," Gomez said.
More than 70 European projects were rejected or restricted in the first four months of 2026 alone, according to theEuropean Data Centre Monitor. Public opposition has delayed or cancelled some $42 billion of data center spending in Europe, accordingto a reportfrom consulting firm STL Partners.
The groups share tactics. After activists in the UK used crowdfunding to launch a successful legal effort to stop a large data center northwest of London, Gomez said she and other Spanish activists were inspired to do the same.
It took them only a week to raise the money they needed to mount what they say is the first major legal challenge in Spain against data center expansion, in this instance to be prevent the Aragón regional government from allowing Amazon Web Service to build one of its largest data center hubs outside the U.S.
"We are exercising our rights," said Luis Garcia from Ecologistas in Acción,one of the groups involved in the case.  "We know they have way more means than we do. But the crowdfunding proves we have gathered a lot of support from so many people, individuals, organizations."
The movement is both global and hyperlocal.
In the tiny village of Cuarte on the rural plains of Aragon, colorful bunting flaps in the wind in the main square beside a Baroque church from a recent celebration by the town's tight-knit community. Strung up on a wall is a giant banner that reads, "We drink water, not data centers."
It's a slogan to protest a giant Amazon facility that's under construction at the edge of the village.
The drilling and hammering of construction interrupts the dawn chorus of the birds. Clouds of dust fill the air and the ground trembles as trucks race piles of freshly dug earth to the site which sits between the village and a protected wetland.
"To us this feels like a seven-headed monster," said Carlos Olivan, a resident of Cuarte. "We're trying, in a very small group, to make visible the scale of what is happening, so people understand, empathise, and mobilize."
The residents began with alocal survey they call a "referendum" in the village, with 144 registered voters – close to the entire voting age population – responding via WhatsApp. 95% of respondents were against these centers. "And we think the other five made a mistake filling out the forms," said Olivan.
The villagers shared the results with local media and took them to town hall meetings and to officials in the regional government. And they want to pressure the authorities to hold a wider referendum to give residents across the entire province a voice in decisions about these data center developments that promise to transform the region.
In all, planning documents show the regional government is processing approvals for 27 data center complexes, one is close to the size of New York City's Central Park. Together it's estimated they'll require many more times the electricity the region currently uses, and consume vast quantities of water in an area already blighted by drought.
David Blasquez, the head of public policy for Amazon Web Services in Spain and Portugal, told NPR the company is doing all it can to be a "best in class" neighbor, including fixing local water pipes to conserve the resource. The regional government told NPR how much water a data center consumes is considered when they weigh planning permission.
But Laura Coscuella, a resident of a town close to where several facilities are planned, said she joined a local group No Es Sequia Es Saqeo – "It's Not Drought, It's Plunder," to fight these developments after learning of the environmental problems some U.S. communities have faced. "We have a lot of data from the U.S. especially. We need everyone to know about this. I'm afraid that people won't notice what is happening until it's too late – until the taps are not working because they have run the water dry."
Coscuella is helping residents of Cuarte become even more effective in their opposition by using strategies in part learned from this wider coordinated network. Each resident plays to their strength, be it searching complex planning documents or planning direct actions.
At the protest in downtown Zaragoza in Aragon, local activist María Peña Calvo said when dealing with companies sensitive to public opinion, every act of opposition matters even if it feels small. "Putting stones in their path can make some companies simply give up or go elsewhere."

title: Can Jensen Huang's departure help Nvidia's competitors catch up?
text: Nvidia has long been the kingpin of the semiconductor industry – a company whose huge technological bets paid off, making its microchips the most in-demand in the world.But now that its CEO Jensen Huang is out amid an alleged spying and extramarital affair scandal, will the shake-up leave an opening for Nvidia’s competitors to catch up?In this episode, we dive deep on the strategies that put Nvidia ahead of the pack, and how other companies are positioned in this moment with Dylan Patel, founder and CEO of the AI and semiconductor research firm SemiAnalysis.This episode was produced by Kai McNamee and Connor Donevan, with audio engineering by Ted Mebane. title: Nvidia's interim CEO inherits risky AI bets and a legal mess
text:
A suspected intelligence scandal, reports of multiple extramarital affairs and the abrupt departure of one of Silicon Valley's most influential CEOs. It's been a dizzying week for Nvidia and the AI industry.
Jensen Huang helped bankroll the AI boom. Now, after 33 years at the helm of the leading company in AI, he's out, leaving questions about the future of an industry that has relied heavily on his company's financial backing. Longtime finance chief Colette Kress has stepped in as interim CEO.
"Nvidia has put itself basically in a position of being a bank, backstopping everything," Gary Marcus, a cognitive scientist and longtime AI researcher, toldMorning Edition.
He was describing circular financing: Nvidia invests in AI companies that then use the money to buy Nvidia's chips. OpenAI, Anthropic and CoreWeave have relied on that funding, he said, even as many AI businesses struggle to turn a profit.
"Jensen was kind of a swashbuckler, willing to make bets of arbitrary size," Marcus said.
Unlike Huang, whose background is in engineering, Kress comes from finance and appears more cautious about making large financial bets, potentially changing how Nvidia backs the wider AI industry.
Kress will also have to contend with potential federal and congressional investigations into Nvidia's dealings involving China, leaving her to "clean up that mess," Marcus said.
He said lawmakers need answers about what information Huang may have shared with Alice Huang and why Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had not intervened earlier.
"Why didn't Lutnick shut some of this down when he was asked to?" Marcus said.

title: They attended Trump's meme coin dinner.  It didn't go well
text:
Headed to what some have called "themost exclusivedinner in the world," hosted by President Trump, crypto investorMorten Christensen and his young sister Gabriëlle Felen had butterflies in their stomachs.
The dinner on Sunday, Nov. 22, was meant to reward the top holders of the president's meme coin — a type of crypto currency that Trump had launched just days before his inauguration.
"I'm excited!," said Christensen. "It's always nice to dress up for an event. My sister looks amazing!"
Christensen — the founder of a crypto websitecalled Airdrop Alert— is a veteran trader who got the crypto bug as far back as 2013. He has attended each of the previous two events Trump has held for the top holders of his meme coin.
For him it was just a chance to get a glimpse of the president. Christensen said that he's not political — and always advises others to "never buy a political meme coin ever."
The events have been intensely controversial. Anti-corruption activists have said they pose enormous conflicts of interest concerns, effectively rewarding those who buy the most coins with access to the president. Top buyers get the closest access.
Christensen was unsure if he would attend this latest dinner. But a sharp drop in the value of Trump's meme coin — from a peak of over $70 in January 2025 tonow less than a dollar— had sharply reduced the cost of qualifying as a top holder, which provides access to the dinner.
And, above all, it was a chance to bring his sister Felen for the ride.
On Sunday night, Christensen and Felen agreed to provide NPR with voice memos through an event that turned out to be something they likely won't forget.
Their butterflies started in the Uber ride to the Trump National Golf Club in Potomac Falls, Virginia. They wanted to head there early. By the time they cleared security, the large room was still filling in.
One of the first things Felen — a recent college graduate — saw was the gift boxes: They contained perfumes, a watch — and a small golden statue of President Trump.
"Pretty nice, pretty nice," said an excited Felen.
The excitement was short-lived.
Christensen bought enough meme coins to qualify as a VIP guest — but when he tried to access the area reserved for the top guests he was denied entry. He was told his name was not on the list.
"Apparently I got removed from the VIP list and I don't know," Christensen said, adding he had even gotten email confirmation.
"But I'm still at the event, so it's all good. It's just a shame."
Perhaps the most controversial aspect of Trump's meme coin dinners is thatmany of the top buyersof the meme coin were believed to have been foreign citizens — raising concerns they could be trying to court influence with the president.
Christensen described meeting many people from abroad at his dinner. Among the people he met were two people who said they work for top crypto exchange Binance.
"One was from Saudi, one was from London," he said.
He met others from abroad as well.
"I met a couple of people from Ukraine. Two people from India. Four from China. I think one was from South Korea," he added.
Christensen and Felen are themselves foreign nationals — hailing from the Netherlands, though they both currently live in Mexico, where they manage Christensen's website.
Consumer advocacy group Public Citizen saidin a reportthat about half of the people who qualified for Sunday's event appeared to be foreign based.
Dinner started promptly with a choice between grilled filet mignon and pan-seared halibut for the main course.
Both Felen and Christensen said they were having fun. MentalistLior Suchard— a special guest at the event — approached them and played a trick. He had Felen write down the name of her first crush on a piece of paper and place it in Christensen's pocket.
Suchard said he would guess the name — and he nailed it — to Felen's delight.
To their excitement, the other top guests such as Kevin O'Leary from CNBC'sShark Tank, former boxer Floyd Mayweather and former NBA star Tristan Thompson also gave speeches.
Just as the night was kicking off, with Felen and Christensen anticipating Trump's appearance — a big problem presented itself.
Christensen was kicked out.
He was approached by a couple people and told he must leave. Christensen said he was told it was because he's been sharing pictures online — and for being in touch with the media.
The organizers did not reply to an email from NPR seeking comment.
It was raining as Christensen stood all the way outside the golf course — still trying to figure out what happened.
"There's a first for everything, and I guess it was at the Trump gala," he said, sounding a little dejected.
The latest Trump meme coin dinner has come amid intense media scrutiny.
The White House has defended the events with meme coin holders as being part of Trump's private business — and not part of his public functions. Trump — who effectively has a royalty deal with the company that runs the meme coin — earned over $600 million last year from the cryptocurrency according to his disclosures.
But the latest event was held just weeks after corruption was a defining issue for voters in the midterm elections, which handed Democrats control of Congress next year.
Prominent Democrats including Sen. Adam Schiff from California and Sen. Richard Blumenthal from Connecticut havedemanded more informationabout the latest meme coin dinner.
Felen and Christensen decided she would stay behind. They figured they came to hear Trump speak and at least one of them should get to do it.
Trump finally made his appearance to big cheers from the crowd. It wasn't a focused speech, Felen said.
"He jumped from topic to topic. It was interesting but just him rambling," Felen said. "Speaking, speaking, speaking — but not making a lot of important points I guess."
For Felen though, it was still a moment to finally see the president.
Felen — and "soaking wet" Christensen — made their way to the hotel. Christensen tried to sound philosophical.
"It happens, you know. It was a different experience this time around. Could have been better, but I will just laugh about it," he said. "All good. It's part of the game."
Heading to the airport to catch their flights out of the U.S., Felen and Christensen were still trying to process the night.
Felen still can't believe she got to go.
"My friends and people who know me from my village are like how did you end up here?," she said.
Nonetheless, both of them sounded more subdued. Felen said she wished her brother had a better night.
"I was definitely disappointed for him, especially later when I saw some people who were VIP actually get, like, a one-on-one selfie with Trump, probably also got to shake his hand," she added. "So that would have been a great opportunity for Morten."
As for Christensen, he said all he wanted was a chance to meet Trump, stressing again that he's not political.
Waiting to catch their flight, he was still unsure of how to feel about Trump's latest meme coin dinner. He does know, though, this will be his last.
"That's a wrap on me on the Trump events," he said.

title: How the high cost of fuel is affecting Thanksgiving travel
text:
Stay up to date with ourUp Firstnewsletter, sent every weekday morning.
The biggest Thanksgiving expense isn't the turkey. Or the cranberry sauce.
It's the cost of travel.
And this Thanksgiving, those costs are going to be higher thanks to fuel prices that have been elevated ever since the U.S. began its war in Iran in February.
Crude oil, which refineries process into gasoline, diesel and jet fuel, has been in shorter supply as the Strait of Hormuz has been effectively throttled. That's meant less oil for refineries to process and higher prices for all of their products.
On Monday,a gallon of gasolinecost 56 cents more, on average, than it did at this time last year. That's a few cents shy of being the most expensive gas priceseveraround Thanksgiving, according to AAA.
Most Americans who travel at Thanksgiving drive, the group noted. Its forecast predicts that a near-record number of people — some81.5 million— will travel at least 50 miles from home for the holiday. Another 200,000 drivers, they estimated, would skip the long-distance road trip this year due to fuel prices.
But Patrick De Haan, the head of petroleum analysis at the fuel-savings app GasBuddy, said that even if drivers aren't happy about gas prices, most of them will still hit the road.
"Thanksgiving is a very big holiday to spend with friends and loved ones," he said. "I don't think that fuel prices are going to be really impeding many people."
Airfare is also more expensive this season. Tickets for Thanksgiving are up about 30%compared to last year,according tothe travel tech company Hopper, and AAAnotedthat the average round-trip ticket in the U.S. this season is around $800.
That's because of the cost of jet fuel. It's one of airlines' biggest expenses, and they're paying billions of dollars more for it this year.
The industry trade group Airlines for America said carriers are eatingsomeof those increased costs. But they'realsopassing some of them on, said Hayley Berg, lead economist at Hopper. "Jet fuel prices are almost 90% higher than they were at this time last year, and airlines have been managing that major cost increase by passing some of those costs onto travelers in the form of higher airfares," she said.
At the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum last week, Delta's CEO Ed BastiansaidDelta's ticket prices are up 15 to 20% this year — and customers are still buying. "Obviously, fuel prices were the trigger that enabled it, but we would not be able to generate that type of pricing if we didn't have a consumer that was willing to pay it," he said.
Berg said that people are willing to shell out, even if plane tickets cost more than they did last year, because they want to stick to their Thanksgiving family routines. "A lot of Americans see their holiday travel as inflexible," she said. "It's either a long-awaited, long-planned vacation or a trip home for the holidays to see friends and family."
Indeed, the TSA says it expects to screen awhopping 17.6 million passengers between tomorrow and next Monday.On Sunday alone, the agency says, it could screen more than 3 million air travelers.
That's despite major problems that have snarled air travel recently in the U.S., including a systems issue that briefly grounded Delta planes in Atlanta over the weekend, and a nationwide ground stop earlier this month caused by an FAA technical problem.
Thanksgiving is Amtrak'sbusiest season— Last year, the rail service broke ridership records during the Thanksgiving travel period, up nearly 6% from the previous year. Amtrak predicts 2026 will be another record year.
Thanksgiving is also a major travel season for buses. Data from Flix North America, which owns Greyhound,showsbookings for the week up 17% compared to last year. Flix says bus fares have a competitive edge over other modes of transportation, which is a big draw for people concerned about affordability.
Fred Ferguson, president and CEO of the American Bus Association, told NPR that Peter Pan Bus Lines is adding more than 300 departures in the Northeast for Thanksgiving. "The company expects to carry more than 160,000 passengers over the holiday, up 7% from last Thanksgiving," he wrote.
December is another huge travel month in the U.S., and the good news for drivers is that although gasoline is still more expensive than it was at this time last year, its price has beendropping in recent weeks.
A gallon of regular now costs $3.63 on average, after hovering above $4 for much of the year.
That's thanks to both seasonal and geopolitical reasons.
Gas tends to be cheaper in the winter. Lots of people take vacation in the summer, so demand — and prices — tend to rise then. Also, refineries make two blends of gasoline. The summer blend produces less smog, but it's more expensive. The winter blend uses butane, which helps cars start in freezing weather, and it's cheaper.
Another major factor is that crude oil prices are falling, because the world's getting more of it out of the Middle East via pipelines instead of going through the Strait of Hormuz. That has meant more oil to go around, which ultimately lowers prices.
Market watchers were also bracing for an escalation of the war in Iran, which some worried could happen right after the U.S. midterms. Since that has not materialized, oil traders are behaving with cautious optimism that the conflict will eventually end, and the strait will reopen. As a result, the price of crude oil has come down off its highs from earlier this year, and that's driving down the price of gasoline.
But the war isn't over yet. Analysts say that even if there was a peace deal tomorrow, it would take many months for the oil supply chain to recover — and for fuel prices to reach their pre-war levels. And while prices are falling now, they're volatile. They could easily swing back up if the war escalates.
Plus, lots of people have already booked their December travel. For them, these high autumn prices are already baked in.
Joel Rose and Scott Horsley contributed to this report.

title: Seniors embrace Tesla automated driving technology despite questions about safety
text:
EVERGREEN, Colo. — Joan Spalding has driven the steep, winding road that leads to her house outside Denver for more than 50 years. But these days, the 89-year-old barely touches the steering wheel or the pedals.
Instead she tells the car where she wants to go, and presses a button on the large touch-screen in the dashboard of her Tesla Model Y.
"I just get in and go," Spalding says.
For all practical purposes, the car appears to be driving itself, navigating confidently on twisting roads through postcard valleys full of juniper and ponderosa pine.
"Now this is probably one of the narrowest roads," Spalding says, as the car pulls onto a dirt track that can barely fit two cars side by side, with a steep drop off to one side.
The Tesla handles the tight turns gracefully, even stopping to let an SUV squeeze by in the other lane.
Spalding was skeptical at first of what Tesla officially calls Full-Self Driving (Supervised), often abbreviated as FSD. It's a subscription service that drivers pay for, usually $99 dollars per month.
That was, until she saw what it could do.
"When I was driving," Spalding said, "I saw that the kind of things that it did were safer than what I would do."
There are more older drivers on the road than ever, and families often struggle with the question of when it's time to stop driving. Now, seniors are using emerging technology to stay behind the wheel longer, specifically automated systems made by Tesla. But safety experts worry the company may be over-selling what its cars can do.
"It's not a technology that I would drive with. It's not a technology that I would suggest that my loved ones use. I think it has a few safety gaps that just make me uncomfortable," said Bryan Reimer, a research scientist at MIT, who studies how drivers interact with technology.
It's hard to know exactly how many seniors are using Tesla's automated driving system, but the numbers may be growing. Overall, Tesla says FSD hasmore than 1.7 million active subscriptions, an increase of 67% from a year ago. If the car-maker knows how many of those subscribers are seniors, it isn't saying.
Riding along with Joan Spalding, it's easy to understand the appeal for older drivers. The car gives her mobility and freedom that she wouldn't have otherwise.
Before she got her Tesla, Spalding had gotten into a number of minor fender benders. Then, two years ago, she was in a serious crash while she was trying to make a left turn.
"I made a wrong decision. I wasn't focusing on what I should be doing … I was lucky," she said. "But I realized then that my abilities were not where I wanted them to be."
Her son Mike Spalding had known for a while that his mother's driving was getting worse. He was already driving a Tesla, and it was his idea to get one for her.
"It would be safer for mom if she was in a wreck because it's got all kinds of safety features. And then safer for people around her if we didn't have any more crashes. I've been driving one for years, and so I'd experimented with the Full Self-Driving and saw what it could do," Spalding said. "It's better than me."
Tesla agrees. The companyclaimsthat FSD is up to nine times safer than human driving. Tesla doesn't release much data about FSD, so it's impossible to independently verify whether its safety claims are true, Reimer said. He concedes Tesla's technology is impressive and is getting better all the time, but says it's not a replacement for a human driver — at least, not yet.
"Tesla has continually over-promised and under-delivered," Reimer said. "Full self-driving is not full self-driving, but yet the name feels so real."
If you read the fine print, FSD is not fully autonomous. The company always uses its full title — FSD (Supervised) — in official communications, to underscore the point. The driver is supposed to be paying attention at all times, in case the car encounters a situation FSD can't handle.
The problem, according to safety experts, is that human drivers tend to get complacent.
"It's good enough, often enough, where people go, 'The next time I'm in this similar situation, I know how it's going to behave,'" said Alexandra Mueller, a senior research scientist at the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, the nonprofit funded by the insurance industry.
But Mueller worries older drivers won't be ready or able to take control of the car in an emergency.
"This can be a huge problem," she said. "Ultimately it is very unsafe if you have drivers who are not fully competent due to age-related impairments or decline."
Tesla did not reply to requests for comment.
The company has not said exactly how many senior drivers are using FSD to stay on the road longer, or even if that's something Tesla is tracking. But the company's CEO, Elon Musk, has encouraged the practice.
In a recent post on his social media platform X, Musksaidthat "Tesla self-driving gives mobility to seniors." Several times, he's amplified a video from a YouTube channel called TFLEV, featuring a 98-year-old man, who just bought his first Tesla.
"It has not made a mistake. And I've been driving it probably two or three months and it's not made an error in its driving, " the driver, Larry Dimmock, said in the video. "In fact, the other day it stopped. A chipmunk was crossing the road and there was no other traffic and it did not run over the chipmunk."
Muskrepostedthe video last month, saying, "At Tesla, we even care about the chipmunks." The clip has been viewed more than 3.5 million times.
"My moment of fame, I guess," Dimmock joked in an interview with NPR.
Dimmock says he's owned dozens of cars in his life, starting with a Ford Model A. He says he's still a pretty good driver at 98 — but not as good as his Tesla.
"I feel safer riding with this auto system than I do driving or riding with anybody. It's just been flawless," Dimmock said. "I'll get in the car and go somewhere, otherwise, I probably wouldn't."
For Joan Spalding in Colorado, it's more than just a question of convenience. She says FSD is allowing her to live independently in the house that she and her late husband built more than 50 years ago.
"I love the solitude of being in that place and being by myself," she said.
Without the mobility that FSD gives her, Spalding said, she would likely have to find another place to live where she wouldn't need to drive.
"I'd have to move," she said. "This way, I think I can drive it for as long as I want to. I don't see any reason why not."
