title: He expected a small-business loan. He got a 7-year nightmare
text:
GLENDALE, Calif. — Sitting at his desk, tucked into a corner of his teenage bedroom — a place where he'd never intended to return, well into middle age — Vahe Shahinian rereads the emails that split his life into before and after.
A broker was offering to fund Shahinian's small business with a line of credit worth $750,000.
It was 2019, and Shahinian's company soared, like a miniature Live Nation-Ticketmaster, selling tickets and producing concerts around Los Angeles and beyond. He imagined how much he could do with stable funding.
The pitch had a catch: Shahinian would first accept a third of the sum and start paying it back immediately, in daily installments of $3,600. After 30 days, he could access the rest of the money. He crunched the numbers, followed up with questions — and took the deal.
Shahinian sent the daily payments, he says, for 30 days. Then 40. Then 50.
The line of credit never came.
"From that day," he says, "it's been one long day, one long nightmare."
For seven years, Shahinian has been mired in the shadowy industry that is now the fastest-growing source of funding for small business in the United States. It's largely unregulated, promising fast money at a tremendous cost. And Shahinian's lawsuitagainst his funderscould become one of the first of its kind to go to trial.
Before the "incident," as Shahinian calls his fateful deal, he'd been in business for 15 years, building his company from a side hustle into his main source of income.
Educated as a computer scientist, he'd spent years programming satellites as an aerospace engineer. In 2004, he also developed a site for something he loved in his spare time: community events. Shahinian called his platform for ticketing and seating charts It's My Seat.
Over a decade, Shahinian grew his business from selling tickets to galas and festivals to producing his own shows: booking artists and venues, promoting and marketing. His first concert, by a flamenco guitarist, sold 400 seats. The next, 700. Three years later, 1960s crooner Engelbert Humperdinck performed for 3,000. In 2015, Shahinian expanded again, into touring.
Like most U.S. small businesses, Shahinian says, he self-funded for years. Entrepreneurs like him often dip into savings, family money or home equity; many run up credit cards and reinvest profits.
Shahinian says he had qualified for several generous credit cards, including an American Express with essentially no spending limit. Later, Amex also repeatedly approved him for special merchant financing: instant short-term loans with a low interest rate of 6%.
"All my life," Shahinian offers as his frequent disclaimer these days, "I had never had one missed payment."
By 2018, Shahinian says, he had built his retirement plan: His ticket sales climbed toward $5 million a year, his profits $250,000.
Booking his biggest tour yet, with a 1980s German superstar, Shahinian sought his fifth round of Amex merchant funding.
Except this time, Amex said no. The company was phasing out the program.
All Shahinian could think was: "Whoa." Tours are costly affairs with down payments to venues, marketing, airfare, lights and sound. He'd left himself no time to maneuver — two weeks to acquire about $200,000.
Enter merchant cash advances.
Small businesses in the U.S. consistently say they turn to merchant cash advances, MCAs, because they find few alternatives, especially in an emergency.
Most traditional lending takes months and vigorous vetting. The Small Business Administration hastightened its lending rules. Big banks reject about 20% of business loan applications, according to theTreasury Department, and respond to a quarter with only partial funding. A recentFederal Reserve surveyfound even lower odds.
MCAs, by contrast, present themselves as a lifeline, offering large sums within hours.
Their fees, however, runfrom 25% to 200%and more, when translated into an annual rate. MCA firms argue they charge a lot because they take on big risks.
They also face almost no regulatory oversight.
MCAs escape most lending laws because, technically, they are not loans. An MCA is meant to be a purchase of future sales — a business gets cash in exchange for a steady cut of its earnings later. MCA funders generally aren't required to be licensed and face no legal limit to how much they can charge.
The industry runs the gamut: A funder could be a firm recommended by Amazon, or the latest fintech startup, or a former subprime mortgage lender. Some rely on brokers to drum up deals. Most collect payment by withdrawing directly from their borrowers' bank accounts — often daily.
Shahinian, scrambling after the Amex rejection, lined up two cash advances for a total of $250,000, he says, owing back almost $400,000. This saved his concert tour but cost him all the profits.
"It was my fault — I waited last minute," Shahinian says. "I'm talking to myself, 'Vahe, you had to do it this time. You're never going back to MCAs.'"
But MCA pitchesnever stop. Sometimes, Shahinian replied that he wanted only a traditional loan, something along an 8% interest rate.
Before he even went hunting, the offer came to him — the pitch that changed his life: The line of credit up to $750,000 at an annual interest rate just under 9%. Finally, Shahinian thought, someone recognized the quality of his business.
"It's like the puzzle fit, you know?" he says.
This encounter took Shahinian beyond the MCAs' unforgiving fees into what he alleges was fraud.
As he weighed the offer's condition — 30 days of daily $3,600 payments — he didn't recognize it as a merchant cash advance.
On the phone, the broker presented it as a routine test, Shahinian says, to show his dependability before he'd qualify for his preapproved line of credit. Shahinian had no lawyer or adviser to consult then. He looked up the finance firm, Wall Street-based EIN Cap; it advertised itself as a "provider of working capital to local businesses."
"I was assured that 'We've done this for years. We don't care about a 30-day program — our goal is long term,'" Shahinian says. "The whole setup was to make someone like me feel assured, feel safe — and I felt safe to go in it."
From the start, Shahinian says, he received $228,000 instead of the promised $250,000. The difference was withheld as an initial fee, a common feature of MCAs. He set aside almost half the funds to secure his daily $3,600 payment. The rest vanished into down payments for venues and other tour investments.
After 30 days, when the line of credit didn't materialize, Shahinian says the broker portrayed the delays as technical. His emails grew urgent.
"I had calculated and planned everything based on the 30-day plan."
"I planned massive tour projects based on this solid word. This is not a joke."
"I don't think you understand the urgency of this situation. I'm basically out of time."
EIN Cap later in court argued it never promised Shahinian any loans or lines of credit — only a merchant cash advance, which it delivered. EIN Cap said it was the brokers — the middlemen — who had arranged the deal and made promises. Much of what the company had to say about its ties to those brokers is in sealed depositions.
After 40 days of daily payments, Shahinian says, for the first time, his bank account hit zero.
Shahinian's lawyer, Shane Heskin — who has been clashing with MCA companies for a decade — calls what happened here "carroting." As in, a carrot gets dangled in front of a small-business owner in the form of an attractive financing deal — a low-interest loan — in a bait and switch to sign an unsolicited MCA.
"I see two or three a week," Heskin says about such cases. "They're exploding."
Heskin says common targets are first-time business owners, first-time borrowers and especially immigrants.
NPR spoke with several entrepreneurs who were "carroted" in similar ways. One described falling into a deep depression; another declared bankruptcy. None, except Shahinian, wanted to speak on the record.
Shahinian says he paid his unwanted MCA to the end, hemorrhaging cash.
"That's just who I am, you know?" he says, explaining his choice. "Who I was."
In fact, had he stopped paying, his funders might have sued him for debt collection — acommon consequence with MCAs.
Days before his biggest concert tour yet, with his accounts empty, Shahinian assessed costs: venues still half-paid, airfare unbooked and rising in price, thousands of tickets undermarketed and unsold.
He did what many business owners do when they struggle to stay afloat with merchant cash advances: He took out more cash advances.
Shahinian says his two new MCAs, totaling around $250,000, evaporated into expenses in half a day.
"From here," he says, "the avalanche of money over money, over money, over money started."
He tapped his credit and then home equity — his own, his parents' and his best friend's. Within weeks, Shahinian says, he was more than $1 million in debt to friends and family.
"He asked me for some money, and, I mean, I could see he's drowning, you know?" says Zorik Yeghikian,who did lend to Shahinian later on. He's arestaurant owner whom Shahinian had helped win a catering contract for a local concert venue.
Yeghikian knew the trap of MCA payments. They had nearly capsized his own business, he says, when he'd borrowed about $30,000 and owed nearly triple. Yeghikian slept at his restaurant and worked double shifts alongside his wife, both forgoing pay.
"I lost my hair," Yeghikian says. "I went through hell those years."
The exact scale of the MCA industry is unclear, but it's ballooning. TheFederal Reserve Bank of Kansas City reportsthat businesses are increasingly turning to MCAs to cover basic expenses like payroll. MCAs are a frequent feature in small-business bankruptcies, whichhave been rising.
Shahinian canceled several concerts of his tours, costing him six-figure losses. Many shows went underpromoted and undersold. They might have seemed OK to the audience but did little to save him.
He began to default on his debts.
Shahinian watched himself become someone who lost count of overdue bills and unpaid invoices. He tapped more emergency MCAs and raked in collections notices. Some of his clients received lien letters, asking them to redirect any payments meant for Shahinian to his funders instead. His business relationships wore thin. His social circle shrunk.
He huddled in his home office with his tuxedo cats, Koby and Toby, and faced the existential dilemma: fight or flight?
Shahinian's choice — to fight — is rare. Borrowers often struggle to afford lawyers, let alone find one familiar with the MCA industry.
And MCA firms can be difficult to pin down. Shahinian says he had to hire a private investigator to reach his funders to serve his lawsuit.
He sued EIN Cap and the brokers in 2019. Threeyears later, he settled his claims against the brokers to focus on EIN. His remaining case in U.S. District Court in Los Angeles accuses EIN of fraud.
"EIN Cap denies Mr. Shahinian's claims, and its position is set out in its public court filings," Levi Silver, counsel for EIN, said in an emailed statement, declining any further comment due to the pending case.
As Shahinian's lawsuit plodded through the legal system, he descended down its rabbit hole.
"Most people settle, but no one depended on this promise like I did, to this magnitude," Shahinian says. "There's no way I was gonna go down. I decided to fight it to the end."
He scoured the web for people associated with his lending deal.
He found his broker, who'd introduced himself as Bryan Stein, used different names andbeen indictedfor financial crimes. The Brooklyn District Attorney's Office told NPR that the man, Boris Shteyngart, pleaded guilty in 2012 to grand larceny; public records show he served time in prison.
Shahinian spent a year tracking down some 700 business owners who'd been sued by EIN for debt collection.
Most did not want to revisit that chapter. Shahinian says that he connected with 70 and that many "came to tears" because "someone is standing up to bullies."
In the past decade, EIN has faced several lawsuits in at least nine states, records show. Most cases related to bankruptcies by its MCA borrowers, and most were settled or dismissed. In one case in Washington state, EIN was ordered to return the daily fees it continued to withdraw from a business that was already insolvent.
Last year, a U.S. district judge in Illinois ruled against EIN in a case over its 2019 MCA funding to a firm thatfederal regulators accuseof running a Ponzi-like scheme. The judge wrote that EIN "propped up" and "prolonged the Ponzi scheme" by either failing to conduct due diligence or ignoring its findings, and must return profits of $184,854.
Meanwhile in California, Shahinian's trial was delayed by another nine months. Shortly after, he lost his house to a foreclosure.
For 16 years, Shahinian lived in a lush suburban cul-de-sac in the vibrant Armenian American community of Glendale, north of downtown Los Angeles. In front of his former house is an ancient oak tree; the backyard spills onto the foot of a mountain.
At age 51, Shahinian sold off belongings, packed up his cats, computer screens, ticket printers and prized sound system — and moved in with his elderly parents.
Every dollar from the foreclosure sale, Shahinian says, went to pay mortgage debt and part of the debt to his best friend.
Several friends have urged him to move on from his costly seven-year legal fight, perhaps declare bankruptcy. To him, that's admitting defeat.
"My fault," he says, "was only believing in a promise that I could have never imagined to be false."
In recent years, a handful of states, including California, have started requiring MCA companies to be clearer, in writing, about their fees. And California recently alsopassed a lawthat, starting in 2028, will require funders and brokers to be licensed and undergo background checks and inspections.
It's too late for Shahinian.
His business is now back to basics: ticketing, mostly for local shows, and coding bells and whistles for his marketing software. He hopes his lawsuit will recoup more than $5 million — all the debt Shahinian estimates he has accrued since his "incident," including some $3 million in interest and fees.
He lays blame for its entirety at the feet of his funders, with a car-accident comparison. "You're being rear-ended," he says. "The 12-wheeler rear-ending you, you lose the steering wheel, and you smash into a bunch of cars, and everyone's focus is: Why did you smash into a bunch of cars?"
Heskin, Shahinian's lawyer, says the best-case scenario would be a multimillion-dollar judgment with punitive damages, "and then it's good luck collecting on it."
He's not sure what assets EIN or its employees named in Shahinian's lawsuit still have. NPR asked EIN's lawyers whether the firm still operates; they didn't respond. The firm's investors are unknown.
Shahinian argues any win would be meaningful.
"It would show everyone [whom] I affected these years that I'm in the right," he says. "Hopefully it would be a case for the industry to self-heal, self-correct. Maybe. And it'll be hope for others who are stuck — give them motivation."
"Don't give up, you know?" he says. "Don't be on path of least resistance. Go fighting."
He chuckles and pumps his fist up in the air.
NPR's Will Chase contributed to this report.

title: You Can Seize Everything (The U.S. is reviving pirate law)
text:
The U.S. is working on bringing back the ancient maritime practice of prize law — which allowed for privateers, or more recently, navies, to seize enemy-linked ships, and quickly sell them off.
Why? Well, the U.S. has been seizing lots of big boats — oil tankers linked to Iran and Venezuela — in what the Pentagon calls an effort to disrupt 'illicit networks.' But after they seize the big boats, they have a big problem: Boats are very expensive to maintain, and each day the government owns them adds extra costs. So they want to sell off the tankers and the oil inside as soon as possible.
On today's show, pirates, some swashbuckling, and an interview with the federal judge tasked with standing up a modern-day prize court.

title: How exactly did Trump get so rich on crypto? We explain
text:
For the last year, Will Ragland and a team of researchers at the Center for American Progress — a left-leaning think tank in Washington, D.C. — have dedicated themselves to countinghow much moneyPresident Trump and his family have made in his second term.
So far, they put the total at nearly $3 billion. More than 2 billion dollars of the earnings come from cryptocurrency ventures.
"You could probably combine all of the past presidents' income made during their time in office," Ragland says. "And it wouldn't come close to what we're seeing here."
This unprecedented profit could soon become a major political problem for the president.
After campaigning heavily on an anti-corruption message that resonated with voters, Democrats are promising to make holding Trump and his administration accountablea critical plankof their oversight agenda when they take over both the Senate and the House next year.
FromSen. Elizabeth Warrenfrom Massachusettsto Rep. Robert Garciafrom California, prominent Democrats are vowing to hold oversight hearings and hold President Trump and his administration accountable.
"Americans should be secure in the knowledge that their government is focused on their best interests—not on making the President's family richer," Rep. Garcia warnedin a letterafter the midterms this month warning Trump, his family and his administration to preserve records.
Here's a guide to how Trump made his crypto wealth.
Shortly before his inauguration in early 2025, Trump and now-First Lady Melania Trump each launched their own meme coins — or cryptocurrencies based on Internet memes, cartoon characters, or even jokes.
Trump made over $600 million from the meme coin called $TRUMP, according to the president's own disclosures.
In an effort to drum up demand for the coin, Trump also held two galas for the top holders of $TRUMP. The president promised the closest access to himself to those who invested the most in the coin.
A third gala is scheduled for Sunday at his golf course in Virginia.
Many of the guests for the first event last year were likely tohave been foreign, according to media reports. The second dinner, held this year, attractedconsiderably less interest, though participants also described a significant presence ofpeople from abroad.
For Ragland and other anti-corruption activists, the dinners raise significant concerns about potential conflicts of interest.
"This is a way for foreign investors, foreign countries in some instances, to try and get as much influence as they can and use that as leverage for deals that they want to make that are helpful to them," Ragland says.
Already, top Democrats including Rep.Jamie Raskinfrom Maryland havelaunched investigations— and the galas are likely to become an aspect of their oversight into Trump's crypto ventures next year.
A White House spokesperson warned Democrats against pursuing "sham investigations" when contacted by NPR about the Democrats' oversight plans.
"As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans," Lauren Bis said in an emailed statement. "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."
But the biggest source of Trump's wealth over his second term comes from a crypto venture called World Liberty Financial, which the president's family helped launch even before Trump won the 2024 presidential election.
Working with Steve Witkoff — whom Trump would later appoint as U.S. envoy for the Middle East — as well as Witkoff's son Zack Witkoff, the Trump family started World Liberty Financiallate in 2024.
The venture revolves around a type of cryptocurrency called stablecoin (here'san NPR explainer). Zach Witkoff now serves as the CEO of World Liberty Financial.
Just days before Trump's inauguration, World Liberty received a $500 million investment in exchange for 49% of the company.
The buyer? A firm linked to Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, a member of the United Arab Emirates royal family who serves as the kingdom's national security adviser. The news wasfirst reportedby The Wall Street Journal.
The investment was an extraordinary show of faith in a young company that was striving to get a foothold in the crypto sector.
Months later, the U.A.E. earned a substantial concession: The U.S. eased export restrictions, allowing the shipment of about 500,000 of the most advanced American AI chips to the kingdom. The shipmentwas criticalin the U.A.E's ambition to build big AI data clusters and become an AI power.
Democratshave seized on the timing, although President Trump has denied any quid pro quo. In a recent interview with CBS'60 Minutes,the president said he does not keep track of how much money he makes from his business ventures.
"I devote almost no time to my net worth. I don't care. I make – I have a lotta money, and far more than I ever thought I'd have. And I guess it's gone up. I don't even know,"Trump told60 Minutescorrespondent Ross Douthat.
But Will Ragland and his team have tallied up the earnings linked to World Liberty Financial and its stablecoin business: The total, they say, is over $1.7 billion.
World Liberty Financial declined to comment.
Another key deal with World Liberty Financial helped boost the profile of the company's cryptocurrency — and the Trump family's profits.
Using$2 billionof World Liberty Financial's stablecoin, a separate firm — also led by Sheikh Tahnoon — bought a small stake in a top crypto exchange called Binance last year.
The deal instantly elevated World Liberty Financial's stablecoin into one of the biggest in the market.
Months later, Changpeng Zhao — the convicted founder of Binance who no longer runs the crypto exchange —was pardonedby President Trump. CZ, as he's widely known, still has the biggest stake in Binance and weighs in publicly, including when theexchange got hackedearlier this month.
Meanwhile, the relationship between Binance and World Liberty deepened. Binance actively promoted World Liberty Financial's stablecoin to its customers, further elevating the market valuation of the cryptocurrency to $5 billion,according toThe New York Times.
While the relationship has come under scrutiny, Binance has strongly defended the acceptance of World Liberty's cryptocurrency as having been done on its own merits.
"Any suggestion that Binance did anything to support World Liberty Financial or USD1 to gain political favour or influence a legal outcome is false," a spokesperson told NPR in an email, referring to World Liberty's stablecoin. A representative for CZ declined to comment.
But transparency advocates are suspicious — and so are top Democrats. In a widely quoted social message, Rep. Robert Garcia posteda social media messagefor the Trump family and his administration: "Lawyer up."

title: 'Medicare for all' is back on the drawing board. Does it stand a better chance this time?
text:
Check outthe NPR Politics Podcastfor daily analysis of the biggest news out of Washington, D.C.
History doesn't repeat itself, but it does rhyme, as the saying goes. That's certainly true of the coming fight over "Medicare for All."
The midterm elections resulted in victories for several candidates who made universal, government-funded health coverage, or some variation thereof, a central pillar of their campaigns, including new Democratic U.S. senators-elect from Michigan, Maine, Iowa, and Texas. They — and many of their soon-to-be colleagues — say they will push the new Democratic majorities in the House and Senate to finally solve the healthcare affordability problem, which so many voters complained about on the campaign trail.
But while virtually every elected official supports making healthcare available and affordable for all Americans, the details of getting there cleaved the Democratic Party the last several times healthcare topped the national agenda. The Clinton health reform effort in 1993-94 fractured over differences within the Democratic majority, as those who wanted a dramatic overhaul like Medicare for All argued with those who saw incremental changes — such as a public option — as more politically feasible. The Affordable Care Act, which despite incendiary politics made incremental reforms, barely squeaked into law in 2010after similar disputes..
And, so far, it appears history is about to write another stanza of this epic poem.
So why is something so popular in the abstract so hard to accomplish?
For one thing, most Americans have no real idea what the phrase "Medicare for All" actually means. "It's cosplay," said Nicholas Bagley, a law professor at the University of Michigan who has written about health policy for years. "When you say 'Medicare for All,' people think 'Healthcare — good. We should have more of it.'"
Mollyann Brodie — who oversees KFF's public opinion and survey research program as executive vice president and chief operating officer of the health information nonprofit — points out that in the long history of Medicare for All, support rises and falls dramatically depending on how the policy is described to voters.
"I can move it up to three-quarters [percent approval] if I talk about it being a guaranteed right to healthcare or eliminating insurance premiums and reducing out-of-pocket costs," she said of survey respondents' support, on arecent episodeof theWhat the Health? From KFF Health Newspodcast. "I can plummet that support down to the 20s if I talk about it requiring people to pay more in taxes or threatening the current Medicare program."
A second problem Democrats face is that the Medicare program itself, which covers adults 65 and older and some people with disabilities, is on less-than-firm financial footing. As of this year, the trust fund that underpins the hospital insurance part of the program isprojected to become insolvent in 2033.
Costs arerising for Medicare beneficiariesas well. The program requires significant out-of-pocket spending on premiums, deductibles, and coinsurance. At the same time, traditional Medicare fails to cover much-needed services such as dental, vision, hearing, and, most expensively, long-term care. Beefing up Medicare benefits would be expensive and likely require large tax increases, according to most outside estimates.
The new Democratic majorities in Congress will have to decide whether their priority is to reverse the spending cuts made by the Trump administration — both to the Medicaid program for low-income and disabled people and to Affordable Care Act health plans — or to expand coverage and lower costs, turning back time to before President Donald Trump's second term began.
"Expectations are super high among voters right now, and they are demanding action on healthcare costs," Brodie said.
There are already indications that Democratic leaders are listening to the Medicare-for-All wing of their party. A day before being officially nominated as the next speaker of the House, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New Yorkvoiced supportfor expanding government-funded coverage, including by lowering the age of Medicare eligibility and covering all children.
Of course, even if Democrats can pass legislation to restore what was cut by the GOP, there is every expectation that Trump — who has referred to Medicare for All in the past as "a socialist takeover of our healthcare system" — would veto those efforts. And the new majorities, while large, are not veto-proof.
Finally, Democrats must face a reality that both parties often forget: The larger your majority, the more ideologically diverse it will be. While the next Congress will include more progressives pursuing Medicare for All, it will also have plenty more moderate members from swing districts currently represented by Republicans. It's the reverse of the splits that plagued the GOP in the current Congress, with conservatives from safe red districts pitted against moderates from purplish ones.
Thereisone big difference in the coming Democrat-on-Democrat debates compared with those in 1993 and 2009. One thing that has hamstrung Democrats trying to fix the health system is resistance from a plurality, if not a majority, of Americans who are relatively satisfied with their current health coverage. During the Clinton-era health reform debate, those people were represented in the famous "Harry and Louise" ads sponsored by the health insurance industry, featuring a couple at their kitchen table worrying that proposed changes would leave them worse off financially.
KFF's September tracking pollfound instead that not only was the professed support for Medicare for All at its highest since the organization started regularly asking about it, but also a majority of respondents said they would support the policy even if it meant eliminating the private insurance industry. That's a first, and a significant change at that. It suggests the public is so fed up with the status quo that they'd rather risk something completely new than stick with what they have.
Of course, that sentiment could change fast when industry opposition revs up its counter-campaign. Still, the survey results suggest the next health reform debate could start with a public ready for something bigger. Now it's up to the people who could make it happen to get on the same page.
HealthBent, a regular feature of KFF Health News, offers insight into and analysis of policies and politics from KFF Health News chief Washington correspondent Julie Rovner, who has covered health care for more than 40 years.
KFF Health Newsis a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs atKFF— the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

title: How a viral video gave a huge boost to new gene therapy
text:
Sanfilippo syndrome is a rare and degenerative disease that can be fatal by the time someone reaches their teens. So the O'Neill family knew they didn't have much time after learning their 4-year old daughter, Eliza, had it. At the time no treatment existed, and the world of drug development had its eyes on more common illnesses. So the family took an all-hands-on-deck, unusual approach to directly raise money and boost medical research.
NPR pharmaceutical correspondent Sydney Lupkin joins Short Wave to share what happened next, and what she learned from the O'Neills story about thepromisesandchallengesof drug development.

title: More people are getting the flu. Should you get a flu shot before you travel?
text:
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
More people are getting the flu than usual this fall, according to thelatest influenza tracking numbersfrom the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
"Flu started a bit early this year, so it's out there and spreading," says Dr. William Schaffner, aprofessor of infectious diseases at the Vanderbilt University Medical Centerin Nashville, Tennessee. "So people who are thinking of Thanksgiving travel need to get their protection as quickly as possible."
The flu shot takes about ten days to reach its full efficacy, so there's still time to get one before Thanksgiving, Schaffner says. And the sooner someone gets it, the better – especially because people will be gathering in enclosed spaces for the holidays.
AAApredicts that this year, around 82 million people will travel more than 50 miles over Thanksgiving break, including 73 million by car.
Getting the vaccine doesn't mean someone won't get the flu – but it does mean they'll be less likely to wind up in the hospital from influenza-related complications. Those include pneumonia and secondary bacterial infections.
"It can strike a healthy person at any age and put them in the emergency room. Flu is like that," Schaffner says.
People at the highest risk are seniors, young children and people with underlying health conditions.
Schaffner also says not enough people are getting their COVID boosters.
"Somehow they think that COVID has disappeared," he says. "But the people who are admitted to my hospital with COVID are invariably people who are not up to date with their vaccinations, as with flu. That COVID vaccine helps keep you out of the hospital. It is still a threat. It hasn't gone away."
People should have no trouble finding available vaccines for the flu, COVID and the highly contagious respiratory syncytial virus, RSV, at their local pharmacies and health care providers' offices, says Claire Hannan,the executive director of the Association of Immunization Managers, adding that vaccination season is in "full swing."
"Now is definitely the time to get vaccinated," says Hannan. "Influenza is circulating, people are traveling, people are getting ready for Thanksgiving, the holidays. And the best protection you can get is from the vaccine."

title: How bird poop and manta rays sustain a pristine coral reef
text:
Coral reefsare at risk around the world. So how do they stay so healthy on the remote Pacific islands of Palmyra Atoll? The answer might be in bird poop, manta rays and tree saws. NPR's Lauren Sommer recently visited the islands and takes Short Wave on a tour of its conservation secrets and lessons for the rest of the world.

title: Are your body clocks off? Meet ‘circadian depression’
text:
What if depression is sometimes linked to your body's internal sense of time? That's what researchers from the University of Sydney's Brain and Mind Centre wanted to know. In a new study, they surveyed patients with depression whose symptoms may reflect problems with their circadian rhythms – like their sleep schedule, how tired they feel in the morning and whether they're a night owl. They found that about 1 in 4 qualified for what might be termed a circadian subtype of depression. And while there's still a lot of research to be done, this could open up new pathways for mental health treatment. NPR health correspondentWill Stonewalks us through the study and its implications.

title: Far from home, Voyager 1 will soon be a 'light-day' from Earth
text:
NASA's Voyager 1 has traveled farther than anything else that humans have launched into space. On Wednesday, it's set to reach a new milestone: reaching a distance that is one-light day away from Earth.
NASA is celebrating the occasion with the"Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day." Calling it a symbolic celebration, NASA is asking the public on Tuesday night to send Voyager's call sign V-G-R into the sky in morse code. Use a flashlight, phone light or anything that can blink a sequence.
If you want to take part:
V - Three quick flashes, one long flashG - Two long flashes, one quick flashR - One quick flash, one long flash, one quick flash
What exactly is a light-day?
A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, or more than 16 billion miles.
This NASA spacecraft has traveled for nearly 50 years, launching Sept. 5, 1977.
Over the course of its mission, Voyager 1 has conducted flybys of Jupiter and Saturn. In 1979, it discovered a faint ring system on Jupiter. In 1980, the spacecraft took detailed photos of Saturn's rings and moons.
While on its journey, on Feb. 17, 1998, Voyager 1 overtook the U.S. space probe, Pioneer 10, becoming the most distant human-made object in existence. It and its twin, Voyager 2, are the only spacecraft to have operated outside of the heliosphere, which acts like a protective shield of the solar system.
Voyager 1 reached the interstellar boundary in 2012. Its interstellar mission continues to chart and measure the magnetic fields, particles and plasma waves outside the sun's heliosphere and the atmosphere of other stars.
Earlier this year, NASA elected to shut off Voyager 1's Low-energy Charged Particles experiment, or LECP, which has helped scientists map the structure of space, in order to save power. Scientists said this could keep the probe alive longer..
Voyager 1 has two science instruments still running: one that measures magnetic fields and another that listens for plasma waves.
In addition, the Voyager spacecraft is carrying the Golden Record – an interstellar "time capsule" to communicate Earth's story to extraterrestrials.
The gold-plated record contains 115 images, natural sounds such as surf, wind and animals, and spoken greetings in 35 different languages. Included are instructions, in symbols, on how to play the record and the origin of the probe.
Voyager 1 is estimated to reach "light-day status" at 5:16 a.m. ET on Wednesday, after 49 years, two months and 11 days of travel.

title: SpaceX successfully catches Starship and makes history
text:
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — SpaceX's Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday, caught in midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier.
It was the grand finale that Elon Musk and his team hoped for — the first-ever capture of a Starship flying back from space. But with the first-stage booster exploding shortly after Friday's liftoff from Texas, the company fell short of its desired double catch.
Wreckage remained in the Gulf of Mexico, cordoned off by buoys, as the stainless steel, bullet-shaped spacecraft lowered itself upright at the launch pad.
The dramatic, sci-fi-like capture helped blot out the booster's messy miss.
"Can you believe it?" shouted SpaceX commentator Dan Huot.
SpaceX officials said Saturday's catch demonstrates the full reusability of Starship, intended for moon and Mars travel. Although Friday's booster recovery failed, the company had already made three previous booster catches, validating the technique.
NASA welcomed Saturday's news. The space agency is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base. Musk's ambitions are even grander: He wants to launch a fleet of Starships to build a city on Mars.
The world's largest and most powerful rocket — a 407-foot (124-meter) behemoth — blasted off late Friday afternoon from SpaceX's Starship base near the U.S.-Mexican border. Separating neatly from its booster before things went awry, the upper-stage spacecraft soared into orbit and released 26 advanced Starlink satellites.
Starship continued circling the world 165 miles (265 kilometers) up, with live views of itself and Earth streaming down via Starlink. The spacecraft completed 14 laps around Earth, outshining the previous mission's one to two laps.
It was SpaceX's 15th flight of a full-scale Starship since 2023 and its only second trip to orbit.
SpaceX reported that everything on the spacecraft, including its vital heat shield, appeared to work well.
As for the booster, SpaceX's Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon on the way back down. The booster's guidance system sensed it wasn't in the right position and automatically initiated the watery detour and self-destruction. Engineers are still investigating the cause.
SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida's Kennedy Space Center within the next few months. That is the starting point for NASA's next Artemis mission, which will skip the moon and remain in orbit around Earth for lunar lander practice.
Artemis III's four astronauts will attempt to dock their capsule with not only Starship but Blue Origin's Blue Moon. The two companies will take turns delivering crews to the lunar surface. NASA is targeting as soon as 2028 for Artemis IV, humanity's first moon landing since the Apollo era more than half a century ago.

title: A new policy could help solve the U.S. organ shortage. Critics say it's unethical
text:
The U.S. organ transplant system has approved the first national policy for acontroversial procedureused to remove organs from hospital patients. The guidelines are designed to protect potential donors. But critics say they do little to improve safety and fail to address deeply troubling ethical concerns.
Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.
The procedure is called normothermic regional perfusion, known asNRP. It can be used after a family has decided to withdraw care because there's no hope of meaningful recovery for the person. To perform NRP, doctors attach an external pump to a donor minutes after their circulation has ended and they've been declared dead. The pump restores blood flow to their hearts, lungs, kidneys, liver and other organs to keep them from deteriorating.
"The hope with NRP is that it increases the supply of organs and it increases the quality of the organs," says Dr. Raymond Lynch, the director of transplantation at theHealth Resources & Services Administration, the federal agency that oversees the organ transplant system.
NRP could help solve the chronic organ shortage, Lynch says.More than 109,000Americans are waiting for an organ transplant, according to HRSA. About 12 die every day because of a chronic organ shortage.
Critics, however, say NRP is unethical because it violates theDead Donor Rule, which is the most important rule protecting potential donors. The rule says transplant surgeons can only take organs from patients after they are dead because of brain death or circulatory death. But because NRP restarts circulation, critics say the procedure reverses the very condition upon which the person has just been declared dead.
"In order to be dead by circulatory criteria it means we're not going to attempt to reestablish circulation. But that's exactly what they do in NRP," says Dr.Lainie Friedman Ross, a University of Rochester bioethicist. "So, yes, I have a real problem with NRP. I think it violates the dead donor rule. It's taking organs from people who are no longer dead."
The other aspect of NRP that troubles critics is what surgeons do to try to make sure the donor is also brain dead, after circulation has been restarted by a mechanical pump. They clamp off blood vessels that supply the head. But alarm bells started going off for organ retrieval teams when blood appeared to get restored – or "reperfused" – to the brain during some NRP cases.
"We have seen signs of life in NRP when the brain has been reperfused," says Dr. Claire Morgan, a transplant surgeon who serves on the transplant network'sPatient Affairs Committeeand was the first to report such cases to HRSA. "It's extremely disturbing."
Those cases prompted HRSA to instruct the Organ Procurement & Transplantation Network (OPTN), which runs the organ system, to investigate and develop a response. On Nov. 6, the OPTN board of directors approved the first phase of the firstuniform national guidelinesfor how to perform NRP.
The new guidelines, which will go into effect Dec. 6, call for surgeons to do more than just clamp the blood vessels to the brain. They should also cut holes in them, according to the new policy.
"Clamping the blood vessels should stop blood flowing to the brain," says Lynch. "Cutting or venting above the level of the clamping is a second safeguard to make sure that if the clamping is insufficient that it immediately drains out of the head and is not supplying warm oxygenated blood to the brain."
The new policy also includes other protections, including recommending against giving donors drugs that would paralyze them and mask any movements.
But critics say the new safeguards are insufficient. Most surgeons already both clamp and vent blood vessels to the brain, for example, they say.
"I honestly don't believe they have created a policy that creates much or any more protection than these donors already had," says Morgan.
Critics also say the new policy doesn't begin to address the bigger concerns that NRP donors are not technically dead when surgeons remove their organs. They worry the adoption of the policy could speed the use of NRP before the troubling questions have been fully aired.
"I really think the policy is the cart before the horse," says Dr.Matthew DeCamp, a University of Colorado bioethicist. "The fundamental issues around NRP still remain unresolved."
Lynch, however, argues the new guidelines will protect donors and that NRP is ethical.
"This is an important first step to make sure NRP care is available but that the safety of the family's loved one is always at the forefront," Lynch says. "This is life-saving care that will extend the supply and improve the quality of organs that patients can get in transplant. And if it is done properly, it is safe."

title: SpaceX's giant rocket may leave NASA in the dust
text:
Later today, SpaceX is planning the most ambitious test yet of its massive new rocket Starship. If all goes well, it will lift off from a pad in South Texas, circle the Earth and then land vertically at the same pad 22 and a half hours later.
The test would be a major milestone for a rocket that company founder Elon Musk says he hopes will one day carry astronauts to Mars. But experts say the rapid development of Starship could also end up stranding one of the company's biggest boosters over the years: NASA.
That's because as SpaceX ramps up its new rocket, it has said it will stop flying a much smaller one called Falcon 9. Falcon 9 launches the company's Dragon capsule, which is currently the only American spacecraft capable of ferrying NASA astronauts to and from the International Space Station.
"Because Dragon has become such a successful and reliable vehicle, it became the de facto way for astronauts to get to orbit," said Caleb Henry, director of research at Quilty Space, a firm that tracks the space industry.
According toa NASA announcementin September, the space agency has contracted with SpaceX for three additional flights to the International Space Station. That would only allow Dragon to fly through 2028, assuming the missions were flown consecutively in six month increments and no further flights are contracted with SpaceX.
"NASA and SpaceX continue to work closely together across numerous missions and contractual agreements, including crew and cargo transportation to the International Space Station," the space agency said in an e-mail statement to NPR. "As the commercial space industry evolves, so will the technologies and services available to NASA."
The space station is currently set to retire in 2030.
The current problem facing the space agency marks a stark reversal from earlier times, when it was SpaceX that was depending heavily on NASA. In 2008, following multiple failures of the Falcon 9, the space launch company was on the ropes.
"We were running on fumes at that point, we had virtually no money," Elon Musk told CBS' 60 Minutes in a 2014 interview.
Then, just days before Christmas, NASA came through with a big contract.
"I couldn't even hold the phone, I just blurted out, 'I love you guys!'," Musk said.
For the next decade, a steady diet of NASA and eventually Pentagon contracts were responsible for a big share of the company's revenue. But all that changed in 2020, when SpaceX launched a subscription satellite internet service called Starlink. Starlink subscriptions quickly eclipsed the money made from launching rockets.
Today, according to SpaceX'slatest financial report, the company made around $2.1 billion in revenue from space launches through September of this year. By contrast, Starlink pulled in around $12.8 billion, while its rapidly growing AI business made around $10.9 billion.
Starship is central to SpaceX's newer, larger businesses. The space launch company is already using it to send its new, powerful V3 satellites for Starlink into orbit. Further down the road, Musk has said he wants the rocket to deliver data centers to space.
"Once Starship is flying reliably several times per week, it makes sense to shift super scarce SpaceX engineering and production resources to Starship to get launch rate to several times per day, which means winding down Falcon," Musk saidon Xearlier this year.
"We definitely want to move from the older technology to the newer technology," SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell said at the All In summit in Los Angeles in September. "A Falcon 9 with a Dragon capsule on top is like a minivan. … The road trip to Mars is six months — so you don't want to be in the minivan."
The problem is that the minivan is perfect for taking astronauts on a short jaunt to the space station. In fact, it's currently the only American option for making the trip.
Henry said building space capsules is time-consuming and expensive. And as it turns out NASA is about the only one willing to pay, making it a very small market for a company like the one SpaceX has become.
"Today there is not a strong commercial market for human spaceflight," he said.
The retirement of the Falcon rocket will have huge impacts beyond human spaceflight. A recent analysis by Quilty Space finds that the commercial market may end up short by some 150 launches between now and 2030, and the Pentagon hasreportedlybeen left scrambling to find rides for national security satellites. In a statement to NPR, the U.S. Space Force said it had secured Falcon 9 launches through 2028 and that it was "confident" other suppliers would be able to pick up the slack.
None of that is likely to change SpaceX's mind, according to Tim Farrar, the president of TMF associates, a telecom analysis firm that tracks SpaceX.
The company has grown far beyond its launch business, he said. "SpaceX has now got an enormous amount on its plate."
In particular, "it's not making a lot of money out of NASA," he said. "Although it seems likely that the individual missions are profitable, they're small potatoes."
It's still not clear when SpaceX will retire the Falcon 9 rocket. The company did not respond to NPR's request for comment, but in her public comments at the summit, Shotwell implied that a rival company, Boeing, could fly to the station instead.
"Boeing has been paid, I think, probably more than we have been paid to develop their human capsule. So we're just going to let them have some business," she said. "They should fly their capsule."
The Boeing capsule, known as the Starliner, has been beset by problems throughout its development. In 2024, failures with the vehicle's first attempt to take astronauts to space resulted in a planned eight-day mission aboard the ISS becoming a nine-month stay. The astronauts returned home on a SpaceX vehicle in March of the following year. The next Starliner test flight is set to take place over the winter, with a crewed flight sometime in 2028.
For Farrar, SpaceX's choices make sense for its business, but he wonders whether NASA deserves better. "They were responsible essentially for SpaceX not going bankrupt," he said. "One would hope that there's a bit of loyalty."

title: AI could help hospitals diagnose PTSD in real time
text:
Every year, millions of people in the United States develop PTSD from a traumatic event—like a car crash, an assault or freak accident. A lot of those people end up in the ER answering the same question: "What brought you to the emergency department today?" Now, a research team in New York has an AI model that can use patients' answers and demographics to spit out one number that tells medical staff how likely a patient is to develop PTSD a month later.
The work – published in the journalNature Communications– could help an often-overloaded emergency department team prevent mental health disorders before they start.

title: Can scientists reverse your age?
text:
Reversing aging may sound like science fiction, but scientists have already found a way to do it—at least, theoretically. Based on a 2012 Nobel-prize winning discovery, researchers are testing whether they can revert diseased cells in the eye back to young and healthy ones. They gave people a drug this year. If it works, it'll open the door to curing and possibly preventing other age-related diseases. And that led producerBerly McCoyto wonder: Could all this research eventually extend our human lifespans?

title: How this year's record El Niño could hit your wallet
text:
Peru's anchovy industry, the largest single-species fishery in the world, is being rocked by the ongoing El Niño . It's not the first time the fishery has been impacted by the natural weather phenomenon — El Niño gets its name from Peruvian fishermen. And it's a stark reminder of the reverberating economic consequences of El Niño events, which can cost the global economytrillions of dollars.

title: He was diagnosed with cancer. Then he was told he lost his Medicaid
text:
Eli McCreary of Omaha, Neb., said he had recently been diagnosed with kidney cancer when he got a call from a local hospital run by CHI Health. He said he was informed that he wasn't insured anymore under Medicaid — and that the hospital would cancel his appointments unless he paid out-of-pocket.
McCreary, who was 64 at the time, said he phoned a call center for help. He said he was told his benefits under Medicaid, the government health program for people with low incomes or disabilities, now required that he have a job.
"You're required to do work to stay on," McCreary said a representative told him. "And you haven't fulfilled your work requirement."
Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.
For decades, McCreary said, he has battled drug addiction. A substance use treatment program discharged him in March, and in June he was diagnosed with cancer in his right kidney, according to documents reviewed by KFF Health News. He also has diabetes and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
"I don't understand what job I can get," McCreary said. "I can't walk. I can hardly breathe. I can't move around. What job am I going to get?"
McCreary said he canceled a CT scan and other tests at the hospital, which is part of CommonSpirit Health, the nation's largest Catholic health system. He also delayed a cancer-related appointment with a physician who travels back and forth to Omaha. "I missed my window of opportunity with him for another month," he said.
Taylor Miller, a spokesperson for CHI Health, declined to answer questions about McCreary's experience. In an emailed statement, she said that "CHI Health is committed to helping patients understand their health care coverage and access to care, including available financial assistance resources."
Determined to be the first state to enforce Medicaid work requirements under President Trump's signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Nebraska launched the new rules May 1 — eight months before most states are set to do the same. With their newly elected majorities in Congress, Democrats have said they plan to repeal the changes to Medicaid in their first 100 hours in office in January. But it is unclear if they will be successful, because Trump could veto it.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillensaid in Decemberthat state officials "certainly appreciate President Trump and his whole administration for delivering this key reform." Pillen spoke alongside a videoed-in Mehmet Oz, the Trump administration official overseeing Medicare and Medicaid.
"We're excited to be able to be the first to make it happen," the Republican governor said.
Laura Strimple, a spokesperson for the governor, didn't respond to requests for comment. Jeff Powell, a spokesperson for Nebraska's Department of Health and Human Services, said its rollout "has been very successful." He pointed tostate data showing86% of affected applicants met the requirement or qualified for an exclusion and 93% of existing enrollees kept their coverage.
Health clinics and organizations advocating for poor and working-class Nebraskans say the rollout has been rife with problems — many due to poor training and inadequate staffing.
About 70,000adult Medicaid recipients in Nebraska are subject to the work requirements. They must prove they're working or participating in a similar activity for 80 hours a month, unless they qualify for an exemption. State officials and consultants advising them have said the May 1 date was challenging to meet.
To deploy the law's Medicaid coverage restrictions, Nebraska budgeted millions of dollars for government contractors, according to state documents KFF Health News obtained via a public records request. Documents from Nebraska's health department outline $8.2 million in contractor costs to enact Medicaid changes, including work requirements and more frequent checks for whether people still qualify.
Nebraska operates the information technology system that determines who in the state qualifies for Medicaid, unlike most states,which outsource the workto companies under contracts often worth hundreds of millions of dollars. But Nebraska's health department nonetheless relies on the private sector to help administer its Medicaid program.
The $8.2 million in costs span two years. They stem from two companies that Nebraska uses to increase agency staffing: Public Consulting Group, based in Boston, and Atlanta-based Covendis, which supplies information technology staffers.
One of the companies has praised Nebraska's implementation of work requirements.A poston Public Consulting Group's website quotes senior consultant Latanya Michaux.
"I really cannot brag enough about how well Nebraska handled this requirement," Michaux said, crediting the firm's "incredible relationship" with the state.
Covendis executives did not respond to requests for comment. Powell said the health department "uses contracted staff when hiring a state employee is either uneconomical or impractical because of time constraints, or when the role requires highly specialized skill sets."
Advocates who work with Medicaid enrollees in Nebraska say that participants are confused and don't know whether the rules apply to them. These advocates say enrollees also have gotten inaccurate information. In December, Pillen said the state "won't be adding workforce" to implement the work requirements, a decision those advocates have criticized. Pillen in July also instituted agovernment-wide hiring freeze.
Nebraska listed at least half a dozen contractors costing more than $250,000 each, including one person whose compensation exceeds $1.8 million, the documents show. Nebraska submitted the records to federal Medicaid regulators as part of a routine process to secure federal money. Powell said the funding requests "may not reflect actual expenditures."
Sarah Maresh, a program director with the social justice advocacy nonprofit Nebraska Appleseed, said the amounts were "shocking."
"When you put in complicated policies like this, there are large corporations making money behind the scenes," Maresh said. "This just further confirms that it's happening in Nebraska quietly."
The Medicaid work requirements in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and other changes shepherded by Republicans will curtail insurance gains that came from the Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare. The GOP tax and spending law, which the Congressional Budget Office estimated would reduce federal Medicaid spending by more than $900 billion over a decade, adds reporting requirements and restrictions that make it harder for people to stay enrolled.
As of early July, most denials related to the work requirements among Nebraska adults applying for Medicaid were due to unsubmitted paperwork, according tointernal documentsfrom Nebraska's health department that KFF Health News obtained through a public records request. The state wrote this was "expected."
State data shows that average wait times at a Nebraska health department call centernearly doubledbetween May and July, going from about 13 minutes to 26 minutes, before declining in August. In interviews, advocates for Medicaid enrollees said they've encountered people who have waited on the phone for hours.
Nebraska receivedmore than 101,000 callsin August, a 66% jump from May.
"If people are working, they just don't have time to be sitting on the phone to go through all of this stuff," said Kenny McMorris, CEO of the Charles Drew Health Center, a federally qualified health center in North Omaha. He said roughly half of Charles Drew's 13,385 patients are on Medicaid, and of those, 42% are subject to the work requirements.
"You can leverage the technology, but you still got to have people there to help," McMorris said.
Then there are experiences the official data may not catch, like what happened to McCreary — saddled with figuring out what happened with his Medicaid benefits amid a health crisis, and whether it was even true that he had to work to keep them.
McCreary had heard about the Medicaid work requirements but didn't know they might apply to him. Powell confirmed McCreary was eligible for Medicaid because of the ACA — putting him in the population subject to work requirements.
His ordeal underscores the fallout from being caught in confusing government systems and silos that aren't obvious to the public.
"This cancer ain't going to stop just because I ain't got insurance," he said. "It's going to keep working on me."
When he received the call from the hospital about his coverage, "I was really in despair," McCreary said. Eventually, he said, he called for help.
Nebraska's health department runs AccessNebraska, a call center for help with safety net benefits such as Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, commonly known as food stamps. But the number McCreary recalls dialing ended up not being AccessNebraska — it was for a different call center, one for SNAP accounts that Nebraska outsources to a private company. Powell said the state has no record of McCreary calling the health department.
McCreary said the worker didn't have a good explanation for why the Medicaid work requirements would apply to him. Before his health deteriorated, McCreary worked as a driver for an asphalt services company. He said he worked "until I couldn't do the job anymore."
"I really had hoped to work longer," he said. "I kind of enjoyed that job."
Attorneys and policy professionals who work with people on Medicaid and other public benefit programs said that McCreary's substance use treatment, lasting four months starting in November 2025, and other health conditions should have exempted him.
The federal law outlines categories of exemptions, such as being too sick to work. People who are considered too ill include those who have a serious medical condition or a substance use disorder.
Nebraska's health departmentsaid it senttens of thousands of letters, text messages and emails to inform enrollees about the new requirements. According to state documents, Nebraska said it would "implement enhancements" to its computer system and online portal, including allowing people to submit documents online and having "clear, plain-language" enrollee notices. McCreary, however, doesn't have an account on Nebraska Medicaid's online portal, preferring to handle things over the phone or in person.
He also said it's possible he missed letters from Nebraska Medicaid about his coverage.
"I don't know if it's my fault or not," McCreary said.
The Cornhusker State's experience could be a harbinger of things to come. Next year, work requirements will apply to millions of adult Medicaid enrollees in more than 40 states.
The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office has estimated the policy will lead to 5.3 million more people being uninsured in the U.S. by 2034.
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Medicaid changes are the most complicated in years — changes that government benefit experts say will strain and exacerbatelong-standing problemswith state technology systems for health benefits.
"It's already a shaky system, and now you've added more burdens on top of that," said Gelila Selassie, director of health advocacy for the nonprofit Justice in Aging.
Nebraska and federal officials, as well as consultants advising the state, detailed the difficulties and successes with the state's May 1 launch during an August panel discussion at a national conference in Oregon.
"They said, 'We're going to go live May 1.' To which CMS said, 'Oh, my God!'" Brent Weaver, an official who specializes in Medicaid IT at the U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, said about Nebraska.
Nebraska officials knew "they weren't as agile as they probably would have liked to have been," Weaver said, "but they didn't let that stop them."
"If they fail, we looked at it as a failure," he added in comments that broadly praised the state's approach.
CMS did not answer questions from KFF Health News about Nebraska's rollout and Weaver's remarks.
In Nebraska, a group of 60 people held hours-long meetings three days a week that were "very exhausting," Michaux, of Public Consulting Group, said during a different session at the conference.
"Our calendars were cleared, and that was the focus," Michaux said.
Because CMS had not yet issued regulations outlining key details such as how people could get exemptions — it would do so June 1 — Nebraska officials said they had to rely on the law's broad language to make initial decisions.
"We had to get comfortable being uncomfortable," Jacob Kawamoto, a deputy director at Nebraska's Medicaid division, said at the conference.
Public Consulting Group said it worked with the state to developnew guidance and "process guides"— materials for Nebraska eligibility workers with instructions on how to process Medicaid applications or renewals. Training materials for Nebraska caseworkers reviewed by KFF Health News refer to those guides.
"The training was very robust, and the process guides were very robust," Michaux said.
Maresh disagreed with that characterization. "There are gaps" in the state's training materials, she said, and caseworkers "are confused" about work requirements.
Public Consulting Group also helped the state institute changes to Nebraska's Medicaid IT system,according to the company. "We are preparing for future updates and enhancements," Michaux said.
In response to questions, Public Consulting Group spokesperson Alyssa Brown said the company "has supported Nebraska Medicaid via a broad range of consulting services since 2019, including work on federal and state compliance initiatives." She said Michaux "discussed" the process guides at the conference but Nebraska developed them. Similarly, Brown said the company did not develop training.
Federal taxpayers will largely bear the costs of implementing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Medicaid policies in Nebraska and elsewhere. Congress allocated $200 million in one-time funding to states. Under federal regulations, the U.S. government picks up most of the tab for state IT system changes, paying as much as 90% of the cost.
"Even though it was not so easy," Michaux said at the conference, "we definitely had fun standing up the Medicaid work requirement program."
Public Consulting Group's employees, Brown told KFF Health News, are "passionate about public service and helping our clients improve the lives of the people they serve."
As of August,roughly 1,100 Nebraskanshad been denied benefits because of Medicaid work requirements. Most denials were because people did not respond to requests for information.
Nebraska's total Medicaid enrollment has declined by roughly 4,600 people since May, a drop of 1.4%, according to anAugust report.
As for McCreary, the Nebraska health department's Powell maintained he experienced "no lapses in coverage" and said he was disenrolled from Medicaid after turning 65. Despite what McCreary said he was told, Powell said Medicaid work requirements weren't the reason: He aged out of Medicaid and into Medicare before they could be applied to him.
Selassie, from the nonprofit Justice in Aging, said McCreary's care shouldn't have been disrupted.
McCreary is now enrolled in Medicare, and Medicaid covers some of his health costs. He was able to reschedule his canceled appointments.
"The cancer has grown so much," he said.
He had surgery in early November to remove his right kidney.

title: NASA is looking for astronauts to live and work on the Moon
text:
If you have dreams of going to the moon, you now have a chance. NASA is accepting applications for those interested in becoming an astronaut.
The candidates selected to be astronauts would not only test spacecraft but would also live and work on the moon in a future moon base, said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman in a statement released on Saturday.
"Those missions will demand technical excellence, sound judgment, teamwork, and courage," the statement said. "NASA's astronaut corps has always called on remarkable Americans willing to take on extraordinary challenges in service to the nation."
There are currently 32 active astronauts in NASA's astronaut corps. Since NASA missions began in the 1960s, the agency has selected 370 people to train as astronauts, according to the agency.
The applicant process is extremely competitive. Out of more than 8,000 applicants for NASA's last astronaut class, only 10 candidates were selected.
While any U.S. citizen can apply and there is no official age restriction, applicants will need to have a master's degree in a STEM-related field such as engineering or math.
In a recent change, a nursing degree qualifies.
"Nursing degrees are now included in the STEM definition," Anna Schneider, NASA spokesperson, told NPR on Sunday. "Master's-level nursing degrees now meet the minimum educational requirement, whereas nursing degrees were previously excluded."
In addition, NASA is requiring a minimum of three years of related professional experience after completing a degree.
In lieu of a master's degree and working experience, NASA will consider those in a PhD program (in STEM), doctors or pilots with extensive flight experience.
If chosen, the selected astronauts will undergo training that will last for two years. NASA said astronauts will prepare for critical and difficult missions such as landing near the moon's South Pole.
To achieve its goal of returning humans to the moon in 2028 – the first time since 1972 – NASA is relying on private companies such as Blue Origin and SpaceX to develop systems and spacecraft.
During a Nov. 7 press conference on the Artemis III moon mission's progress, Isaacman said he is "very confident" the mission will launch in 2027.
The starting salary is $164,395 and applications will be received through Dec. 3.

title: How climate change transforms the colors of our world
text:
Imagine the bright tones of coral under the sea. What do you see? What colors come tomind?
One of the ways that climate change will alter â or has already altered â our world is by shifting the familiar colors of nature. When warming ocean waters bleach the vibrant colors of coral to white, thatâs oneexample.
âMany young scientists who are working on coral reefs donât realize that what theyâre seeing is vastly degraded,â says Anya Salih, a scientist who has studied coral reefs and their fluorescent colors for decades. âItâs often hard to perceive how it was to what it isnow.â
This change of color isnât just aesthetic. For coral, bleaching leaves them vulnerable to disease and other stressors that can lead to death. In other situations, these color changes have more complex impacts, ones that scientists are still trying tounderstand.
An illustrated journey
A shifting landscape in theArctic
Every summer, massive climate-driven wildfires spreadsootacross huge swaths of the Arctic, covering the ice in a blanket of black particles. Soot pollution from oil and gas operations, as well as commercial shipping and increased tourism, contributes to the problem at bothpoles.
The dark particles coat white snow and soak up heat from the sun, exacerbating melting that was already happening more quickly because of climate change. Increased melting in the Arctic leads to sea level rise, which threatens communities across the world. And the soot itself pollutes the air and water it seeps into.âWe know that the high northern latitudes are warming faster than the rest of the planet,â says Douglas Morton, an Earth scientist at NASAâs Goddard Space Flight Center. These changes are shifting the colors of the Arcticlandscape.
Source:National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration
Beyond the Arctic ice at the pole, farther south, lie vast regions of permafrost: soil that has remained frozen foryears.
But the warming climate is causing permafrost to thaw.
And in some places, crack and collapse.
As permafrost thaws deeper into the soil, nutrients become more available and plants can grow deeper roots. These conditions can stimulate plant growth and enable larger vegetation like trees to gain a foothold, turning the landscape greener.
These established plants also trap snow in the winter, insulating the plants from the cold and promoting further plant growth.

These established plants also trap snow in the winter, insulating the plants from the cold and promoting further plant growth.
A 2020studyinNature Communicationsused satellite data to estimate Arctic vegetation over time, sampling thousands of sites across Alaska, Canada and western Eurasia. The researchers found that between 1985 and 2016, about 38% of the sites showedgreening.
âNot everywhere in the Arctic is green,â says Logan Berner, a terrestrial ecologist with the University of Alaska Southeast, who led the study. âBut thereâs enough greening that if you look at the average greenness of the Arctic over time, itâs goingup.â
According to Berner, who grew up in southern Alaska, this consistent increase in average greenness tracks strongly with an increase in summertemperatures.

Though the Arctic might seem far away from us, Berner notes that itâs a âbellwether for the kinds of impacts that climate change can have.â And increased greening can negatively impact the people who live in the Arctic and rely on its natural resources. For example, as shrubs expand across northern lands, they can shade out berry patches that people rely on for food; changing weather patterns can also affect the timing of fruit and itsquality.
Changes in ourwater
âPeople have coined the term that lakes are sentinels in the landscape,â says David Butman, a professor at the University of Washington who focuses on biogeochemistry and satellite remote sensing. Lakes react quickly to changes in the environment, so measuring lake color through satellite monitoring can help quantify thosechanges.
Butman worked on a 2021studyinProceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America(PNAS) that measured green wavelengths in more than 400,000 lakes in the boreal Arctic zone in North America. Researchers found that green values declined by 15% between 1984 and 2019, meaning that, to the naked eye, these lakes got significantlydarker.
Thawing permafrost is a possible reason. As it thaws, soil can mix with lake water, making it darker. The researchers found that the greatest declines happened in warmer and wetterregions.
The darker a lake gets, the more heat it can store, according to Butman. âYou can imagine, you know, a black car and a hot day,â he says. The darker a lake is, the longer it stays warm after the summer,disruptingthe natural timings of processes like fish life cycles and algae production. When soil or other outside material sinks to the bottom of a lake, microbes consume oxygen to break it down, leading to the production of methane, a potent planet-heatinggas.
On a global scale, many lakes fall within the green-blue color spectrum. Bright blue lakes, often depicted in illustrations, are rarer than greenlakes.
In 2022, scientists Xiao Yang and Catherine OâReilly led astudyinGeophysical Research Lettersthat analyzed the color of more than 85,000 lakes. They found that blue lakes are generally found in northern places with cooler summers and are covered in ice in the winter, such as Moraine Lake in Canada or Lake Baikal inRussia.
Globally, approximately 31% of the Earthâs lakes areblue.
Yang and OâReilly predict that fewer blue lakes will exist as summers get warmer and winter ice cover decreases due to climatechange.
The birds and thebees
Many animals have appearances that blend in with their surroundings for survival. When those surroundings start to shift, animals such as the snowshoe hare begin to stand out. The snowshoe hareâs white winter fur sticks out with less snow on the ground, leaving it more vulnerable topredators.
Researchers havenât foundevidencethat hares are adapting the timing of their molts to align with their changing winter. But some insects have already changed coloring. North American male dragonflies, for instance, have adapted to warmer climates by losing color on their wings, according to astudyinPNAS.
Losing some of the heat-absorbing color can help the dragonflies stay cooler, but the males also lose color that helps attract females. And researchers predict this will continue to be the case in the future as the climate continues to warm. An even tinier example is a specific kind ofbee.
Sevan Suni is an associate professor at the University of San Francisco who studies interactions between plants and pollinators. She has been going to Costa Rica for the last 15 years to study a group of bees commonly known as orchidbees.
These bees are the sole pollinators for about 200 species of orchids in Central and South America. Their bodies look almost jewel-like, with shiny iridescentshells.
Year after year, Suni noticed that one species of bee, the championâs orchid bee, seemed to shift color from blue-green to orange-red. She and othersdiscoveredthat, in hotter areas, the number of orange-red bees has increased over time while the number of blue-green bees hasdecreased.
The areas that increased in temperature faster over time also had more of the red-orange bees. Itâs unclear whatâs driving this change. The darker blue-green color could be hotter, absorbing more heat. Or the blue-green bees may be more vulnerable since the color of their environment is changing. Due to deforestation in Costa Rica, they may be less camouflaged in a less green environment. Either way, Suni has concerns about potentialimpacts.
âAs a biologist, Iâm always interested in biological variation,â she says. âIt worries me a little bit if the blue-green morph has an important ecological function and theyâre getting less prevalent overtime.â
A last gasp of hiddencolor
Warming ocean waters bleach colorful corals, turning them white. The corals expel symbiotic algae, losing a food source and becoming more vulnerable to disease. Corals can recover after bleaching, but the longer and more frequent the bleaching, the more difficult recovery is. In some cases, corals turn stunningly fluorescent and colorful at the start of bleaching and after â a last bright gasp oflife.
These neon colors, usually visible only under ultraviolet light, are always present to some degree, says Anya Salih. Salih, a fellow at the University of Technology Sydney, has studied coral reefs and their fluorescent colors for decades. She dives at night to scan reefs with bluelights.
âSometimes when I dive with people who are not used to seeing this, I would have to hold their tank so that they donât turn upside down,â she says, âbecause in that very colorful, psychedelic world, you lose the perspective of up and down in thewater.â
